VA-2025-VHA-0073-0004: veterans who need covered abortions benefit from being able to receive them within the va system, optimizing their continuity of care and access to needed support services. changing this rule will harm their health, risk their lives, and damage their relationship with the department. ===== file 0004__1.pdf ===== i formerly served as director of the center for women veterans at the department of veterans affairs (va). i am also a va patient: i choose to get my health care from va because the care i get from my patient-aligned care team is comprehensive and integrated; my provider takes the time to address all my needs. it is also important to me that my providers understand my military-specific risks and exposures; i am screened for military sexual trauma, and my doctor knows what burn pits are. among women veterans using va health care, 43 percent are of reproductive age (18–44). reproductive health needs, such as contraceptive care, pelvic exams, and obstetrics, are one of the top five reasons women veterans of reproductive age seek care from va.i to meet the fundamental health care needs of women veterans, it is important for va to be able to provide the full spectrum of reproductive health care. on july 1, 2020, i testified before this hvac’s subcommittee on health on this topic, recognizing va’s areas of strength while also noting that there were deficits related to provision of in vitro fertilization, contraception, and abortion.ii since that time, va has made significant changes in provision of equitable, lifesaving care, including removing the full exclusion on abortions and abortion counseling from the medical benefits package. the proposed regulation to reinstate it is poor policy that will harm women’s health. the dobbs v. jackson women’s health organization supreme court decision limited some women veterans’ access to the full scope of reproductive health care, as those living in many states no longer have access to abortion care in their communities. this has a direct impact on their health, since abortion can be medically necessary.iii the rule on reproductive health services in place at va since 2022 supports women veterans’ access to needed abortion treatment by removing the exclusion on abortion counseling from the medical benefits package and allowing enrolled veterans “to obtain abortions, if determined needed by a health care professional, when the life or the health of the pregnant veteran would be endangered if the pregnancy were carried to term or the pregnancy is the result of an act of rape or incest.” while not expansive enough to cover all situations in which abortion could be beneficial for enrollees, this rule will protect the lives and health of many vulnerable veterans. having a service-connected disability is a primary way veterans qualify to enroll in vha care, and research has shown that vha users tend to be older, sicker, and of lower socioeconomic status than veteran nonusers.iv va estimates that 72 percent of current veteran vha users who are capable of pregnancy have a service-connected disability rating of 30 percent or higher.v women veterans who use va have high burdens of chronic disease and a significant rate of mental health conditions.vi for example, pregnant women veterans have extremely high rates of depression and often discontinue medications for this and other conditions, such as posttraumatic stress disorder (ptsd), during their pregnancies.vii abortion counseling is especially important to ensure that veterans have accurate and unbiased information to inform health care decisions that are based on their health history and personal circumstances. furthermore, some mental health conditions are associated with worse pregnancy outcomes: women veterans with ptsd are more likely to experience gestational diabetes, preeclampsia, and preterm birth.viii accordingly, it is exceedingly important that they be able to access the care their providers deem medically necessary for their health. restrictions on reproductive health care at the state level mean that women veterans in certain states are no longer able to access such care from non-va providers. to ensure optimal health outcomes for women veterans, va must be able to provide that care. although all states allow abortions to save the life of the woman and most allow abortions for the woman’s health, restrictive abortion policies are having a “chilling effect” that can delay needed care, including treatment for cancer.ix dangerous delays in providing necessary health care are killing women.x providers in some states face prosecution and jail for providing abortion treatment and, given these risks, may delay or deny needed health care for pregnant women.xi access to medication needed for other services can also be affected, as pharmacists are reluctant to fill prescriptions for drugs that can have multiple uses in addition to medical abortions, such as managing miscarriage or treating chronic disease.xii va’s current rule allows veterans to access care their va providers determine is necessary to protect their lives or their health; the proposed rule will subject these patients to all those documented risks. it is also important that va be able to provide these services directly because va provides high-quality, evidence-based, culturally competent care.xiii for example, va trains providers to provide trauma- informed pelvic examinations, which can be particularly important for women veterans who have experienced military sexual trauma. findings from the women’s reproductive health survey show that the majority of active-duty women do not receive contraceptive counseling and may be entering the va health system unaware of the totality of their reproductive health care options.xiv a large percentage also were unable to access their first-choice contraception methods. va providers can be armed with this knowledge to meet the needs of women veterans. it is important for va to be able to provide this care directly because fragmented care can lead to worse health outcomes, particularly for those already at high risk.xv the relatively small number of patients who are likely to qualify for these services are particularly likely to be vulnerable veterans deserving of compassionate, respectful care during a difficult time. in conclusion, veterans who need covered abortions benefit from being able to receive them within the va system, optimizing their continuity of care and access to needed support services. changing this rule will harm their health, risk their lives, and damage their relationship with the department. kayla m. williams u.s. army VA-2025-VHA-0073-0415: my name is kya vulgamott, and i am a senior in the undergraduate public health program at san diego state university (sdsu). sdsu has a prominent reserve officers’ training corps (rotc) program due to its proximity to camp pendleton, and i’ve had the privilege of forming close friendships with several rotc members. over the past five years, i’ve witnessed a significant increase in participation in the rotc program, and i feel compelled to share my concern about the department of veterans affairs’ proposed reinstatement of abortion and abortion counseling exclusions in va and champva medical benefits. i would like to specifically comment on the language found on page 36416 of the federal register, where the term “elective abortion” is used and where it states that abortion will be excluded except when “a physician certifies that the life of the mother would be endangered if the fetus were carried to term.” the rule also asserts, “no state law prohibits treatment for ectopic pregnancies or miscarriages to save the life of a mother.”this language is misleading in the current legal climate. for example, in ohio, women can be charged with fetal manslaughter in certain miscarriage cases, introducing fear and legal uncertainty around accessing care. additionally, the rule only considers physical threats to a pregnant person's life and fails to consider mental health crises, which are a critical part of overall health. the u.s. department of veterans affairs confirms that veterans are at a significantly higher risk of experiencing mental health crises, including depression, ptsd, and substance use disorders, than the civilian population. these factors can influence the viability or outcome of a pregnancy and contribute to increased rates of non-viable pregnancies or the inability to parent a child safely. mental health is not a secondary concern; it is essential to comprehensive, adequate health care. by eliminating access to abortion counseling and services—even in complex mental health circumstances—this proposal neglects the emotional well-being of veterans and their families. it also removes a layer of emotional support that may be vital for people undergoing pregnancy termination, especially in cases of trauma, sexual assault, or service-related psychological injuries. i recommend that the va redefine “life-threatening” illnesses to include conditions that present serious mental health risks, including ptsd, major depression, and suicidal ideation. further, reallocating funding from military weapons development toward military medical training programs would reduce costs of care and improve internal medical capacity. by providing access to medical training, veterans would be almost guaranteed post-service employment for medical personnel trained during military service. access to these trained professionals would strengthen the veteran care pipeline and encourage quality care within va facilities, potentially even on a volunteer basis by those who are no longer active duty. continuing the ideal of volunteer services, the va could establish support groups as an alternative to formal therapy to provide emotional support for veterans navigating reproductive health decisions. the current proposed rule reinstating abortion exclusions under va and champva programs overlooks critical aspects of veterans’ mental health, emotional well-being, and the complex realities of reproductive health care. by addressing only physical danger and excluding emotional and psychological factors, the rule fails to serve the holistic needs of those who have served our nation. i respectfully urge the department of veterans affairs to reconsider its definition of “needed medical services” to include mental health-related pregnancy risks, invest in medical training within the armed forces, and create emotionally supportive networks for veterans navigating reproductive care. thank you for the opportunity to comment on this critical issue.

va-2025-vha-0073-0002 – proposed rule to reinstate va abortion exclusion dear sir or madam: on behalf of national right to life (nrlc), the nation’s oldest and largest pro-life organization, we write in strong support of the department of veterans affairs’ proposed rule to reinstate the long-standing exclusion of abortion and abortion counseling from the va medical benefits package and the civilian health and medical program of the department of veterans affairs (champva). this proposed rule appropriately restores the va’s medical services to align with decades of federal policy, precedent, and ethical healthcare practice. it recognizes the statutory limitations and moral concerns long held by taxpayers and federal lawmakers regarding federal funding of elective abortion. support for the proposed rule for over two decades—from the establishment of the medical benefits package in 1999 until 2022—the va appropriately interpreted abortion services as not “needed” under 38 u.s.c. § 1710. that position reflected both legal prudence and widespread public sentiment. the biden administration, by reversing that stance in 2022, created a de facto entitlement to abortion services at federal expense. by so doing, the biden administration circumvented long-established legal frameworks, ignored state laws, and contradicted the very intent of the supreme court’s decision in dobbs v. jackson women’s health organization, which returned authority over abortion regulation to the states. the proposed rule acknowledges that va has always covered medically necessary care, including interventions for ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage management, and circumstances national right to life comment in support of va-2025-vha-0073-0002 2 where a mother’s life is at risk. the revised language maintains these life-saving exceptions while reinstating the broader prohibition on elective abortion—a line congress has drawn for decades across multiple federal programs, including medicaid, the federal employees health benefits program, and tricare. legal and ethical alignment the va’s authority to define “needed” services under 38 u.s.c. § 1710 is not unlimited and must reflect the legislative and ethical boundaries established by congress. the rule also restores champva coverage to be consistent with tricare policy, which restricts abortion funding except when the mother’s life is endangered. importantly, no state prohibits emergency treatment for conditions like ectopic pregnancy or miscarriage. suggesting otherwise—as the prior administration’s interim final rule did—was both misleading and inflammatory. this proposed rule reaffirms that the va’s role is to provide legitimate, life-affirming medical services to veterans and their families—not to serve as an avenue for taxpayer-subsidized elective abortions. it honors the sacrifice of our veterans without politicizing their care. conclusion national right to life commends the department of veterans affairs for returning to a policy that respects human life, reflects the legal and moral will of congress, and ensures that taxpayer resources are used responsibly and ethically. sincerely, carol tobias madison laclare president director of federal government affairs national right to life national right to life

VA-2025-VHA-0073-2584: see attached file(s) ===== file 2584__1.pdf ===== august 10, 2025 department of veterans affairs 810 vermont avenue nw washington, dc 20420 re: docket no. va-2025-vha-0073 / rin 2900-as31 proposed rule: exclusion of abortion and abortion counseling from va medical benefits dear secretary collins: i am writing to express my serious concerns about the va's proposal to eliminate abortion coverage from the medical benefits package for veterans and champva beneficiaries. after reviewing the proposed rule and its supporting materials, i believe this reversal would be a mistake that ignores both data and the real needs of women who have served our country. the va's justification relies heavily on the fact that fewer women used these services than initially projected, about 140 per year instead of the anticipated 1,000+ ("exclusion of abortion" 2). but this interpretation misses the point entirely. low utilization doesn't necessarily mean low need. has the va considered that women might face significant barriers accessing these services? geographic distance, provider availability, stigma, or simply not knowing the services exist could all explain these numbers. without investigating these factors, the va is making assumptions that could harm veterans. what's particularly troubling is that the va hasn't provided any data about what happened to the 140 women who did receive care under the expanded policy. were their lives improved? were serious health complications prevented? did they avoid financial hardship? these are the questions that matter when determining if a service is "needed." the medical community has extensively studied this issue. the landmark turnaway study, which followed nearly 1,000 women over ten years, found that women denied wanted abortions experienced higher rates of poverty, were more likely to stay with abusive partners, and showed increased anxiety compared to women who received abortion care (foster et al. 956-957). research consistently shows that women who can access comprehensive reproductive healthcare, including abortion services, have better physical health outcomes, greater economic stability, and improved mental health (ralph et al. 78). the va's proposal simply ignores this evidence without explanation. women veterans aren't just statistics, they're individuals who've sacrificed for our country and often carry invisible wounds. one in three women veterans reports experiencing military sexual trauma (kimerling et al. 2438). many live in rural areas hours from the nearest civilian provider. some have service-connected disabilities that make pregnancy particularly risky. these women have earned the right to comprehensive healthcare through their service, and they deserve better than to have their options limited based on political winds rather than medical necessity. the va has built trust with veterans through trauma-informed care and understanding of military culture. for many women veterans, their va provider is the only doctor they trust. taking away services from these providers forces veterans into unfamiliar settings at vulnerable moments. what concerns me most is how this proposal determines what constitutes "needed" medical care. the statutory language hasn't changed since 1999, yet the va's interpretation has flip- flopped based solely on who occupies the white house. this isn't how evidence-based medicine should work. if the va can reverse 23 years of policy, then change it again after just three years, what does this say about the stability and reliability of veteran healthcare? the proposal fails to account for the true costs of this policy change: emergency room visits when routine care is denied, mental health treatment for forced pregnancies, family instability, children growing up in poverty, and perhaps most importantly, the message it sends to women considering military service about how their country will treat them after they've served. studies show that women denied abortions are four times more likely to live below the federal poverty level and three times more likely to be unemployed than women who received abortion care (foster 182-183). instead of this abrupt reversal, i urge the va to take a measured approach. first, study what actually happened during the past three years. interview the women who used these services and those who needed but couldn't access them. analyze the health outcomes, both physical and mental. look at the financial impact on veteran families. second, survey women veterans broadly about their healthcare needs and experiences. don't assume, ask them directly what they need from their va healthcare. third, if changes must be made, ensure that clear exceptions remain for cases involving rape, incest, and threats to maternal health, not just life. the distinction between "life" and "health" may seem semantic in washington, but it can mean everything to a woman facing a pregnancy complication. the american college of obstetricians and gynecologists emphasizes that "pregnancy-related emergencies require immediate, evidence-based medical interventions" and that delays caused by restrictive policies can "jeopardize patient health and safety" (acog). the men and women who have worn our nation's uniform deserve healthcare decisions based on medical evidence and their actual needs, not political ideology. this proposal represents a step backward that will harm veterans who have already given so much. i strongly urge the va to withdraw this proposed rule and maintain the current policy while conducting the thoughtful, evidence-based analysis that such an important decision demands. our veterans answered the call when our nation needed them. now it's our turn to ensure they receive the comprehensive healthcare they've earned, all of it, without politically motivated exclusions. thank you for your consideration of these comments and for your service to our nation's veterans. respectfully, ryan heckman veteran of the u.s. air force 2007-2011 alfred, ny citations 1. american college of obstetricians and gynecologists (acog). "socioeconomic outcomes of women who receive and women who are denied wanted abortions in the united states." american journal of public health, vol. 108, no. 3, 2018, pp. 956-959. 5. kimerling, rachel, et al. "the veterans health administration and military sexual trauma." american journal of public health, vol. 97, no. 12, 2007, pp. 2437-2442. 6. ralph, lauren j., et al. no. 2025-14687, 90 fed. reg. 36415 ===== file 2601__1.pdf ===== federal register comment submitter: ilan adona date: august 12, 2025 proposed rule: reproductive health services a proposed rule by the department of veterans affairs on august 4, 2025 docket no. 2025-14687, 90 fed. reg. 36415 the department of veterans affairs (va) is proposing to “reinstate the full exclusion on abortions and abortion counseling from the medical benefits package” that was previously removed in 2022 (reproductive health services, 2025). this regulatory decision is based on the determination that abortions are not a “needed” service (reproductive health services, 2025). this is concerning to me as a united states citizen and as a woman because i believe that abortion and abortion counseling are needed as much as most other available and va covered medical procedures and counseling. i recommend this proposed rule be discarded because it is unnecessary, and the process of reinstating the rule is a drain on va resources. based on the research provided in the proposed rule and outside research, there is no clear benefit to reinstating the abortion exclusion. the proposed rule cites the va prediction from the september 9, 2022 interim final rule and march 4, 2024 final rule that the “va would provide abortions to more than 1,000 veterans and champva beneficiaries per year,” but in actuality the “average number of veterans who receive abortions from the va is 100 per year, and the average number of champva beneficiaries who receive abortions from the va is 40 per year” (reproductive health services, 2025). additionally, the va states in its proposed rule that the “va has never understood this policy to prohibit providing care to pregnant women in life- threatening circumstances, including treatment for ectopic pregnancies or miscarriages....” and goes on to state that they will provide abortion services in those situations (reproductive health services, 2025). these facts matter for three reasons: 1) the data of va performed abortions do not delineate between those women electing abortions due to life threatening conditions or for another reason. 2) the va is providing over 90 percent fewer abortions than anticipated and has made clear that they would continue performing abortions in certain situations. 3) pregnancy is inherently a potentially life-threatening condition. according to the centers for disease control (cdc) february 2023 health e-stats, 817 women died from maternal causes in 2022 and 669 died from maternal causes in 2023 (2023 health e-stats, 2025). according to this data, the number of abortions performed by the va is highly unlikely to decrease even in the slightest with this proposed rule and therefore, the rule is unnecessary. according to the department of defense’s (dod) 2023 demographics profile of the military community, 19.7% of the total military in 2023 were female (demographics profile of the military community, 2023). the proposed rule states several times that the determining factor for excluding abortions and abortion counseling in the va’s medical plan is that the services are not “needed.” it is true that abortions are not “needed” by 80.3% of the military who are male, but this diminishes the possible medical needs of almost a fifth of the entire military. under champva and va medical coverage, many covered services credibly fall under the not “needed” category defined by this proposed rule because they are elective. in fact, the following are examples of elective services and procedures provided by champva medical coverage: wigs or hairpieces, penile implants, weight loss medication, genetic testing, tubal ligations, and vasectomies (champva guidebook, 2025). there is no specific ban on elective services or procedures under va guidelines, so it is unclear why abortions and abortion counseling should be excluded, especially when the service is infrequently performed. the proposed rule cites dissatisfaction pertaining to “forced taxpayer funding” as a specific reason to exclude abortions, but i cannot imagine that taxpayers are any more sympathetic to “forced taxpayer funding” for penile implants, vasectomies, or weight loss medication (reproductive health services, 2025). the reproductive health services proposed rule costs are a drain on va resources. abortions are not particularly expensive. according to planned parenthood, abortions cost anywhere from $600 to $2,000 depending on the type of abortion (how much does an abortion cost?, 2025). although this is the cost for patients, if estimating on the high end of 100 abortions per year at $2,000 per abortion, the va is averaging $200,000 per year. as the above data depicts, the majority of these abortions will be performed by the va regardless if this proposed rule is implemented or not because they will be performed in life threatening situations. meanwhile, at the time of writing this comment, the reproductive health services proposed rule has received 2,597 comments and this number will likely increase before the september 3, 2025 comment deadline (reproductive health services, 2025). pursuant to administrative procedure act, 5 u.s.c. § 553(c), the va is required to consider each of the comments and even incorporate the considerations into the final rule (administrative procedure act, 2023). the average salary of a va employee is $105,765 (govsalaries.com, 2024). if four employees spend three months reviewing and incorporating comments into the final rule, that task alone will cost the government over $100,000, which is significant at a time when agency staffing and budgets are decreased. given it is likely that regardless of whether this proposed rule is implemented or not, the va will continue to perform on average of 100 abortions a year, the expense of this process is futile. i would also like to comment on the misleading title of this proposed rule - “reproductive health services.” this title does two things. first, it suggests this proposed rule is about providing reproductive health services to military families, personnel, and veterans. the opposite it true as it proposes to remove reproductive health services from beneficiaries that they have previously had access to. secondly, the title deems abortion and abortion counseling as reproductive health services, which suggests they are in fact needed as part of the whole array of other reproductive, pre-natal, and post-natal services provided by the va. language matters. the purpose of this proposed rule, to remove reproductive health services from beneficiaries' coverage, is hidden behind the seemingly innocuous, even positive title. please consider discarding the reproductive health services proposed rule in light of the data and the purpose of the va’s medical coverage. as stated in the proposed rule, abortions are a reproductive health service that are often necessary. unlike abortion services, this proposed rule is unnecessary and a financial burden on the va. references: administrative procedure act, 5 u.s.c. § 5501 et seq. restores mission focus, strengthens legal clarity, and safeguards clinical ethics, while ensuring veterans continue to receive safe, compassionate care in pregnancy‑related crises. mission and legal alignment – the va’s mission is to provide veteran‑centered care without politicizing its services. a clear exclusion reduces moral conflict among providers, fosters trust, and minimizes inconsistent application across facilities. it also protects conscience rights for clinicians and reduces legal and administrative burdens. clinical ethics and safety – this policy aligns with a precautionary ethic toward nascent human life while affirming care for both the veteran and the unborn child when possible. the va should explicitly clarify that treating ectopic pregnancies, managing miscarriage, and addressing life‑threatening complications (e.g., sepsis, hemorrhage, severe preeclampsia) are not considered abortion, preventing delays in urgent care. expanded prenatal, perinatal, and postpartum services—combined with robust mental health, intimate partner violence screening, and practical supports—offer life‑affirming alternatives to abortion. addressing trade‑offs and opposing views – some veterans face traumatic or high‑risk circumstances, including rape, incest, severe fetal anomalies, or serious maternal health complications. to mitigate hardship while maintaining the exclusion: clinical carve‑outs for life‑saving treatment and nonviable conditions like ectopic pregnancy and early pregnancy loss. mental health and trauma‑informed care, especially for sexual assault survivors and families facing perinatal grief. social supports, including housing assistance, employment protections, nutrition resources, and non‑coercive adoption pathways. implementation violence resources, and community partnerships. conclusion – reinstating the exclusion—paired with explicit emergency‑care protections, rigorous training, and comprehensive support systems—respects the va’s ethical commitments, reduces institutional polarization, and safeguards veterans through evidence‑informed, life‑affirming care. i urge finalization of the policy alongside robust, measurable safeguards so no veteran faces pregnancy‑related crises without timely, high‑quality help.
VA-2025-VHA-0073-2897: this proposed rule, va-2025-vha-0073-0002, to reinstate the exclusion of abortion and abortion counseling from the va's medical benefits package and champva, represents a significant step backward in ensuring comprehensive healthcare for veterans and their families. this decision is not merely a technical adjustment; it's a policy change with far-reaching consequences that undermines veterans' well-being and autonomy. first, it is imperative that veterans have access to the full spectrum of healthcare services, including reproductive healthcare, in accordance with their individual needs and choices. excluding abortion and abortion counseling restricts access to crucial healthcare, potentially leading to adverse health outcomes and increased mental health struggles among veterans, notes votevets. such restrictions ignore the complex healthcare needs of veterans and can force individuals to seek care outside the va system, potentially incurring greater costs and risks. second, this proposed rule has the potential for a disproportionately negative impact on women veterans. as the number of women veterans continues to grow, so too does their reliance on the va for healthcare services. limiting access to reproductive healthcare unfairly burdens this vital segment of the veteran population and risks further marginalizing their experiences and needs within the va system. restricting services like cervical cancer screenings, birth control, fertility treatments, maternity support, mammograms, and menopausal care, which could be categorized under the umbrella of "reproductive healthcare," would be a slap in the face to every woman who has served the nation, according to votevets. third, this move raises concerns that ideological considerations are being prioritized over the healthcare needs of veterans. the original decision to remove these exclusions in 2022 was made with the aim of ensuring comprehensive and medically necessary care for veterans. reinstating the exclusions suggests a shift towards allowing political beliefs to dictate access to medically accepted procedures, which is inappropriate and detrimental to the trust veterans place in the va system. decisions regarding healthcare should be driven by medical best practices and the individualized needs of patients, not by political or ideological agendas. finally, the claim that excluding abortion from va services is necessary to ensure only "needed medical services" are provided is problematic. this stance ignores the fact that abortion can be medically necessary to protect the health of the individual, particularly in cases of rape, incest, or when the mother's life is at risk. the va has the authority to provide comprehensive and medically necessary care to veterans, as clearly established in 38 u.s.c. 1710 and 38 cfr 17.38. reinstatement of this exclusion effectively undermines that authority and restricts veterans' access to care that is widely considered medically appropriate. moreover, the proposed rule acknowledges that the exclusion doesn't apply when the life of the mother is endangered, highlighting the inherent tension between a blanket exclusion and the recognition of medical necessity. in conclusion, va-2025-vha-0073-0002 should be rejected. reinstating the exclusion of abortion and abortion counseling from va benefits would be a step backward for veterans' healthcare rights, potentially harming their well-being and disproportionately impacting women veterans. instead, the va should uphold its commitment to providing comprehensive, medically necessary care that respects the autonomy and diverse needs of all those who have served our nation.

VA-2025-VHA-0073-3545: i am a physician, board certified in internal medicine, living in a state with a 6 week abortion ban. here are my comments on proposed rule va-2025-vha-0073-0002. 1. under the proposed rule, as under emtala, any veteran in the us who has a life threatening complication of pregnancy should be able to get emergency care, including abortion if there is no other option. my ob-gyn colleagues specialized in maternal-fetal medicine point out that this care, whether life-saving for both mother and fetus or for mother only, is technically difficult. with this regulation in place, who will be left within the va system with the training and experience to give this care? 2. the proposed rule makes no exception for rape, incest, fatal fetal abnormality, or fetal conditions that are catastrophic to families, but not immediately fatal. some, like congenital zika, are more likely in mothers who have been deployed overseas. this means that, contrary to promises made to our service members, families receiving care under the va system have substantially less healthcare benefits than most americans! it is shocking. congress must devise a workaround for them. 3. there are many medical conditions which are exacerbated by pregnancy. the mother may not die but she may have a disabling complication. these include lupus, epilepsy and severe migraine. other medical conditions are best treated with medications that can cause fetal abnormalities, aka birth defects. these include cancer chemotherapy agents, major psychiatric disorders and rheumatoid arthritis. veterans receiving these medications are advised to use birth control, but no birth control method is 100% safe. good specialty care for these veterans must include counseling about the risks of remaining pregnant. again, give our veterans the standard of care that applies to the civilian population. thank you for your consideration.
VA-2025-VHA-0073-3666: i am writing to express my opposition to the proposed regulation published on august 4, 2025 (rin 2900-as31), which aims to reinstate the exclusion of abortion services and counseling from the va medical benefits package and champva benefits package as specified in 38 cfr part 17. in the first paragraph of the action section, the regulation reinstates a complete exclusion that exceeds reasonable policy by removing coverage even in situations where a veteran's life or health is at risk or where the pregnancy resulted from rape or incest. i passionately encourage the va to maintain at least the conditional exceptions set in 2022 to guarantee that veterans experiencing medical emergencies or trauma can access the care they require. in the second paragraph of the supplementary information section, the justification stems from the assertion that abortion services are not considered “needed” medical services under section 1710 of title 38; however, the term “needed” is not defined and should be interpreted through clinical judgment that is based on current medical standards, as care may be medically warranted in many specific situations. this exclusion will disproportionately affect veterans in rural regions or in states with higher restrictive abortion regulations, many of whom depend on the va as their sole available medical provider. for this reason, the suggested language stating that “scope of coverage shall exclude abortion services and abortion counseling” should be amended to clearly permit exceptions where the attending va healthcare provider considers the treatment medically necessary, especially when the veteran's life, health, or well-being is at risk, or in cases of rape or incest. veterans who have served this country with honor deserve fair access to healthcare, and the proposed reinstatement does not align with the va's mission of ensuring veteran’s health and dignity. i respectfully urge the department to rethink this stance of exclusion and maintain access to vital reproductive health services for veterans and their families.

VA-2025-VHA-0073-4068: i write in strong support of the department of veterans affairs’ proposed rule to reinstate the long-standing exclusion of abortion and abortion counseling from the va medical benefits package and the civilian health and medical program of the department of veterans affairs (champva). this proposed rule restores the va’s medical services to align with decades of federal policy, precedent, and ethical healthcare practice and correctly recognizes the statutory limitations and moral concerns long held by taxpayers and federal lawmakers regarding federal funding of elective abortion. for over two decades—from the establishment of the medical benefits package in 1999 until 2022—the va appropriately interpreted abortion services as not “needed” under 38 u.s.c. § 1710. that position reflected both legal prudence and widespread public sentiment. the biden administration created a de facto entitlement for abortion services at federal expense by reversing that understanding in 2022. by so doing, the biden administration circumvented long-established legal frameworks, ignored state laws, and contradicted the very intent of the supreme court’s decision in dobbs v. jackson women’s health organization, which returned authority over abortion regulation to the states. the proposed rule affirms that va has always covered medically necessary care, including interventions for ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage management, and circumstances where a mother’s life is at risk. the revised language maintains these life-saving exceptions while reinstating the broader prohibition on elective abortion—a line congress has drawn for decades across multiple federal programs, including medicaid, the federal employees health benefits program, and tricare. the va’s authority to define “needed” services under 38 u.s.c. § 1710 is not unlimited and must reflect the legislative and ethical boundaries established by congress. the rule also restores champva coverage to be consistent with tricare policy, which restricts abortion funding except when the mother’s life is endangered. there are no states that prohibits emergency treatment for conditions like ectopic pregnancy or miscarriage. suggesting otherwise—as the prior administration’s interim final rule did—was incorrect and inflammatory. this proposed rule reaffirms that the va’s role is to provide legitimate, life-affirming medical services to veterans and their families—not to serve as an avenue for taxpayer-subsidized elective abortions. the department of veterans affairs is to be commended for returning to a policy that respects human life, reflects the legal and moral will of congress, and ensures that taxpayer resources are used responsibly and ethically. stephanie holden smith alabama policy institute president/ceo
VA-2025-VHA-0073-4271: august 19, 2025 attn: dr. steven l. lieberman, acting under secretary for health department of veterans affairs 810 vermont avenue nw washington, dc 20420 phone: (202) 461-0373 dear acting under secretary lieberman, i am dr. earl stewart, jr. i am an internal medicine physician and serve as the medical director of health equity for a large comprehensive health system in the state of georgia. i have trained in part as a medical student and resident physician at the va medical centers in murfreesboro, tn, nashville, tn, and providence, rhode island. i am the son of a veteran, son-in-law of a veteran, nephew of veterans, and grandson of veterans. i care for many veterans and their family members as a primary care physician in my clinical practice. i am writing on my own behalf to express my strong opposition to the department of veterans affairs’ proposed rule to reinstate the full exclusion on abortions and abortion counseling from the va medical benefits package, as well as the proposed reinstatement of these exclusions for the civilian health and medical program of the department of veterans affairs (champva), both of which were removed in 2022. as a physician dedicated to creating and advancing health equity, i am deeply concerned that reinstating these exclusions would significantly harm the health and well-being of veterans and their families. the evidence is clear that restricting access to abortion services and counseling disproportionately impacts those who already face barriers to care, including women, gender-diverse individuals, and people of color who have served our country. a recent article in jama health forum (doi:10.1001/jamahealthforum.2022.4621) highlights the critical role that the va’s 2022 policy change played in expanding access to essential reproductive health services for veterans, particularly those living in states with restrictive abortion laws. the article underscores that removing these exclusions improved health outcomes and reduced disparities among veterans. research published in contraception (doi:10.1016/j.contraception.2017.09.012) demonstrates that lack of access to abortion services leads to increased health risks, including higher rates of maternal morbidity and mortality. this is especially concerning for veterans, who may have complex medical and mental health needs. the center for reproductive rights (https://reproductiverights.org/fact-sheet-abortion-access-veterans/) provides further evidence that veterans are more likely to experience unintended pregnancies and face unique barriers to reproductive care. denying abortion coverage through va and champva would force many veterans to seek care outside the system, often at great personal and financial cost, or to carry pregnancies to term against their wishes or medical advice. a recent study in the american journal of obstetrics & gynecology (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajog.2024.09.003) found that abortion restrictions are associated with delayed and reduced access to care, leading to worse health outcomes for patients. the american college of obstetricians and gynecologists (acog) also emphasizes in its 2024 committee statement (https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-statement/articles/2024/12/health-care-for-women-and-gender-diverse-active-duty-and-reserve-uniformed-service-members-and-veterans) that comprehensive reproductive health care, including abortion, is essential for the health and readiness of service members and veterans. additionally, research (doi:10.1055/s-0039-1678749) has shown that abortion counseling is a critical component of patient-centered care, supporting informed decision-making and improving mental health outcomes. in summary, reinstating the exclusions on abortion and abortion counseling in va and champva benefits would undermine the health, autonomy, and dignity of veterans and their families. the evidence overwhelmingly supports maintaining access to comprehensive reproductive health care, including abortion and counseling, as a matter of health equity and justice. thank you for considering my testimony in recognition of the reproductive health needs of the veterans who so valiantly protect the freedoms we enjoy and the families that love and support them steadfastly. sincerely, earl stewart, jr., m.d., facp internal medicine physician VA-2025-VHA-0073-8619: i am writing to express my opposition to the proposed regulation published on august 4, 2025 (rin 2900-as31), which aims to reinstate the exclusion of abortion services and counseling from the va medical benefits package and champva benefits package as specified in 38 cfr part 17. this will lead to negatively impact women's health or even result in their deaths. in the first paragraph of the action section, the regulation reinstates a complete exclusion that exceeds reasonable policy by removing coverage even in situations where a veteran's life or health is at risk or where the pregnancy resulted from rape or incest. i passionately encourage the va to maintain at least the conditional exceptions set in 2022 to guarantee that veterans experiencing medical emergencies or trauma can access the care they require. in the second paragraph of the supplementary information section, the justification stems from the assertion that abortion services are not considered “needed” medical services under section 1710 of title 38; however, the term “needed” is not defined and should be interpreted through clinical judgment that is based on current medical standards, as care may be medically warranted in many specific situations. this exclusion will disproportionately affect veterans in rural regions or in states with higher restrictive abortion regulations, many of whom depend on the va as their sole available medical provider. for this reason, the suggested language stating that “scope of coverage shall exclude abortion services and abortion counseling” should be amended to clearly permit exceptions where the attending va healthcare provider considers the treatment medically necessary, especially when the veteran's life, health, or well-being is at risk, or in cases of rape or incest. veterans who have served this country with honor deserve fair access to healthcare, and the proposed reinstatement does not align with the va's mission of ensuring veteran’s health and dignity. i respectfully urge the department to rethink this stance of exclusion and maintain access to vital reproductive health services for veterans and their families.
VA-2025-VHA-0073-9835: douglas collins, secretary u.s. department of veterans affairs 810 vermont avenue nw washington, dc 20420 re: reproductive health services, docket number 2025-14687 to whom it may concern: i am submitting this comment opposing the proposed rule, “reproductive health services.” this proposed rule would rescind veterans’ access to abortion care in cases of rape, incest, or life or health endangerment to the pregnant person. maintaining narrow coverage of abortion care only when a physician certifies that the life of the patient is in danger will cause confusion among providers and jeopardize the lives and health of veterans. i write as an individual committed to reproductive freedom and as a supporter of the american association of university women (aauw), a nonpartisan nonprofit with over 140 years of advocacy for gender equity. aauw is dedicated to ensuring affordable access to contraception and abortion care for all women regardless of location. i share aauw’s belief that everyone has the right to make decisions about their own reproductive lives without government interference. abortion access is vital to women’s ability to control their lives, bodies, and futures. yet this proposed rule would leave over 9 million veterans, including nearly 300,000 women veterans of reproductive age who rely on the veterans health administration, without access to this essential medical care. the proposed rule will further exacerbate the disproportionate harm of abortion restrictions on black women and women of color, who represent two in five female veterans. to strip our nation’s veterans of a fundamental freedom is antithetical to the promise and responsibility of the department of veterans affairs. i urge the department to withdraw the proposed rule that would rescind access to abortion care for veterans and their loved ones. thank you for considering this comment. sincerely, diane johnson

VA-2025-VHA-0073-12052: see attached file(s) ===== file 12052__1.pdf ===== the abortion debate in the united states has reached a new and alarming stage with donald trump’s push to restrict reproductive healthcare at the federal level. while abortion access is already fractured across state lines after the fall of roe v. wade, the idea of a national abortion ban under trump’s leadership would have catastrophic consequences for millions of americans. one group uniquely threatened by these restrictions is veterans — the men and women who served in the armed forces and who, in many 1710, but this interpretation disregards empirical evidence that abortion access has profound economic and health effects on women. women denied abortions experience a 78% increase in debt and an 81% VA-2025-VHA-0073-18670: comment on proposed rule rin 2900-as31 i am a veteran who has benefited from va healthcare and who believes strongly in protecting taxpayer resources. i do not support taxpayer funding for elective abortion services that reverse prior personal decisions. however, i oppose the proposed rule’s removal of coverage for cases of rape, incest, and medically necessary pregnancy care. this rule, if finalized, would harm survivors of military sexual trauma, as well as veterans facing life-threatening or non-viable pregnancies. these circumstances are not “elective”—they are medical crises. denying such care results in higher costs for the system (due to emergency complications), poorer health outcomes, and unnecessary suffering. the evidence is clear: abortion denial has been linked to increased maternal morbidity, higher infant mortality, worsened mental health, greater economic hardship, and prolonged exposure to violent partners. veterans are at unique risk, with nearly four in ten women reporting sexual assault or harassment during service. i urge the va to revise the rule to preserve exceptions for rape, incest, life- or health-endangering pregnancies, and miscarriage/ectopic care. this balance respects taxpayer concerns while fulfilling va’s duty under 38 u.s.c. §1710 to promote the health and well-being of enrolled veterans. for full supporting evidence, please see the attached pdf appendix. respectfully submitted, michael k. harris sr. ===== file 18670__1.pdf ===== supporting evidence ‒ rin 2900-as31 public comment this appendix provides supporting evidence on the health, mental health, and economic outcomes associated with denial of abortion and miscarriage-related healthcare. each citation is drawn from peer-reviewed studies, government reports, or established research institutes. these references are submitted to support my comment opposing the removal of coverage for rape, incest, and medically necessary care under the department of veterans affairs proposed rule rin 2900-as31. maternal and infant health harms • a 2025 jama analysis found higher-than-expected infant mortality rates in states with abortion bans, including ̃478 excess infant deaths (jama 2025). • studies show pregnancy-associated mortality increased ̃8% in ban states after dobbs (university of colorado/university of maryland analysis, 2024). • documented cases show women with previable rupture of membranes or septic miscarriage faced delayed care, resulting in higher risk of sepsis and hemorrhage (kff 2023; jama network open 2023). mental health impacts • the turnaway study (ansirh, ucsf) found women denied abortions experienced more anxiety, stress, and lower self-esteem than those who received care. • over five years, women denied care had worse physical and economic outcomes than women who obtained abortions (ansirh 2018). violence and safety • research shows women denied abortions were more likely to remain in contact with violent partners, while those receiving care were more likely to escape abusive relationships (foster et al., lancet public health 2018). economic consequences • the turnaway study and follow-up analyses show that being denied an abortion increases poverty, debt, and likelihood of eviction. • a 2022 nber working paper confirmed denial of abortion correlates with long-term financial instability for families. system-level harms to healthcare delivery • abortion bans erode ob-gyn training, reduce availability of emergency miscarriage and ectopic care, and create occupational health risks for providers (acog, jama network open 2023). military sexual trauma context • meta-analysis shows ̃38% of women veterans report mst (sexual harassment or assault during service). denying abortion access in mst-related pregnancies conflicts with va’s mandate under 38 u.s.c. §1710. • va resources acknowledge mst prevalence and prioritize trauma-informed care for survivors; coverage carve-outs are essential.
VA-2025-VHA-0073-18671: comment on proposed rule rin 2900-as31 (supplemental submission) i respectfully submit this supplemental comment to emphasize two points: 1. military sexual trauma (mst). nearly 40% of women veterans report experiencing mst during service. forcing survivors of rape or incest to carry a pregnancy is a direct betrayal of va’s commitment to trauma-informed care. eliminating exceptions for rape and incest would retraumatize survivors and undermine trust in the va system that is meant to serve them. 2. taxpayer costs. while i oppose taxpayer funding of elective abortion services, i recognize that denying medically necessary care increases—not decreases—government costs. delayed treatment for non-viable pregnancies, septic miscarriages, or life-threatening conditions leads to longer hospital stays, permanent disabilities, and higher long-term expenses to the va healthcare system. targeted exceptions are fiscally responsible because they prevent these costly emergencies. for these reasons, i urge the va to preserve coverage in cases of rape, incest, life- or health-endangering conditions, and miscarriage/ectopic care. doing so protects mst survivors while also protecting taxpayers from avoidable future costs. respectfully submitted, michael k. harris sr. ===== file 18671__1.pdf ===== supplemental evidence ‒ rin 2900-as31 public comment this supplemental appendix focuses on two specific issues: (1) the prevalence and impact of military sexual trauma (mst) among veterans, and (2) the taxpayer costs associated with denying medically necessary pregnancy care. these points are provided to reinforce my supplemental comment submission. military sexual trauma (mst) • meta-analyses show approximately 38% of women veterans report experiencing mst, including sexual harassment and assault during service (kimerling et al., 2007; wilson, 2019). • va clinical guidance emphasizes the need for trauma-informed care for mst survivors, including sensitive handling of reproductive healthcare (va mst fact sheet, 2023). • denying pregnancy termination options in mst-related cases increases psychological harm and undermines survivor trust in va services. taxpayer costs of denied care • delayed treatment of miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy leads to more severe complications, longer hospital stays, and permanent injuries̶raising costs to the va system (kff 2023; jama network open 2023). • a university of maryland/colorado analysis (2024) showed states with abortion bans saw increased maternal morbidity and infant mortality, both of which carry higher healthcare costs. • the turnaway study and nber analyses found that abortion denial increases long-term economic instability for women and families, which often shifts costs to public safety-net programs. • preventing medical crises with clear exceptions is less costly to taxpayers than responding to emergencies after denial of timely care.

19673__1.docx ===== september 1, 2025 dr. steven l. lieberman under secretary for health department of veterans affairs 810 vermont avenue nw washington, d.c. 20420 submitted electronically attention: comments in response to proposed rule, rin2900-as31 dear under secretary for health dr. lieberman: the national alliance to end sexual violence (“naesv”) joined by the 25 undersigned national and state organizations writes to comment on the department of veterans affairs (“the department” or “va”) proposed rule on reproductive health services (“proposed rule”). naesv is the voice in washington for the 56 state and territorial sexual assault coalitions and 1500 rape crisis centers working to end sexual violence and support survivors. as a committed advocate for survivors of sexual assault, naesv and the undersigned organizations oppose the proposed rule, and ask the va to recognize that reproductive healthcare is necessary for veterans, and especially necessary for veteran survivors of sexual assault. the va provides hospital care and medical services to veterans through the veterans health administration (“vha”) and to veterans’ spouses and dependents through the civilian health and medical program of the department of veterans affairs (“champva”). in 2022, the department amended va regulations to remove the exclusion on abortion counseling and establish exceptions to the exclusion on abortions for veterans and their loved ones, including implementing exceptions for the life or health of the pregnant person and cases where the pregnancy is the result of rape or incest (the “2022 ifr”). the department later finalized this rule in 2024 (the “2024 fr”). although still not perfect, this policy has nevertheless been critical to ensuring that, regardless of the ever-shifting and restrictive landscape of state laws in a post- dobbs world, the more than nine million veterans enrolled in va’s program, as well as dependents and caregivers enrolled in champva, would be able to access life- and health-preserving medical care. now, however, the va’s proposed rule seeks to reinstate the pre-2022 exclusions on abortions and abortion counseling, which, if adopted, would leave veterans and their loved ones without access to abortion counseling or abortions in the case of life or health of the pregnant person and in cases where the pregnancy is the result of rape or incest. naesv and the undersigned organizations oppose this proposal to walk back critical reproductive healthcare for our veterans and their loved ones and disagrees with the va’s determination that such services are “not needed.” ample evidence confirms it is necessary for far too many veterans and their loved ones (as the va previously acknowledged in promulgating the 2022 ifr). specifically, women veterans are at greater risk of sexual assault and intimate partner violence than their civilian counterparts. indeed, one in three women veterans report experiencing military sexual trauma. one study even revealed alarmingly high rates of sexual harassment and assault among female veterans using veterans health administration (vha) services. moreover, research indicates that a significant proportion of post-9/11 women veterans accessing vha reproductive health care—approximately 68.7%—screen positive for military sexual trauma (mst), with 44.9% reporting experiences of military sexual assault. the department cannot ignore these staggering figures of the frequency with which its veterans experience sexual violence, but it also should not ignore the very real health consequences resulting from that sexual assault. according to the most recent national intimate partner and sexual violence survey, 14.9% of female victims of rape become pregnant. moreover, as the department previously found, survivors of military sexual trauma may experience significant health impacts, including ptsd, depression and other mood disorders, and substance abuse disorders. women who are denied abortions and abortion counseling, compared to women who are able to access comprehensive reproductive services, including abortion care, are also more likely to be tethered to an abuser and to be at risk for continued violence, even if they end the romantic relationship. for the veteran and military community, this is especially troubling: the rate of spousal abuse in the military is twice as high as the rate among the national population, and the transition to civilian life may continue or exacerbate intimate partner violence. considering these findings, it is particularly troubling that the proposed rule would explicitly rescind comprehensive health care access for survivors of sexual assault. the proposed rule fails to contend with this evidence or otherwise explain its policy reversal. it does not even address the rape and incest exceptions with any specificity. survivors of sexual violence, who have experienced the devastation of having their bodily autonomy attacked, must have access to the full range of reproductive healthcare services, choices, and options including abortion and, at a minimum, abortion counseling. if after exploring all of her options, a veteran or veteran’s beneficiary that is a victim of any form of sexual violence decides that she cannot go through with a pregnancy resulting from the crime causing her great bodily injury and risking further injury, the va should not further traumatize such victims by barring them from the full range of reproductive healthcare in the healthcare system that was (and currently is) promised to them. sincerely, monika johnson hostler, president & ceo joined by: arizona coalition to end sexual and domestic violence colorado coalition against sexual assault dc coalition against attached comments in response to this proposed rule. ===== file 19837__1.docx ===== august 27, 2025 the honorable douglas a. collins secretary department of veterans affairs 810 vermont avenue, nw washington, dc 20420 the honorable steven l. lieberman, md acting under secretary for health veterans health administration department of veterans affairs 810 vermont avenue, nw washington, dc 20420 submitted electronically via regulations.gov re: reproductive health services dear secretary collins and dr. lieberman, on behalf of the american academy of family physicians (aafp), which represents 128,300 family physicians and medical students across the country, we appreciate the opportunity to comment on the proposed rule on reproductive health services published in the federal register on august 4, 2025. the department of veterans affairs (va) is proposing to rescind the 2022 reproductive health services final rule and reinstate the exclusion of abortion and abortion counseling from the va medical benefits package and the civilian health and medical program of the department of veterans affairs (champva). the aafp urges the va to withdraw this proposed rule and maintain current policy. we strongly support access to comprehensive pregnancy and reproductive health services and believe pregnancy and reproductive health services are essential to general health care and should be covered under all insurance plans. family physicians across the nation provide comprehensive, continuous, and patient-centered reproductive health services. these include contraceptive counseling and provision, pregnancy care, management of early pregnancy loss, abortion care where legally permitted, and preventive screenings. family physicians serve diverse populations, including veterans, and are often the first point of contact for reproductive health needs. this proposed rule would severely limit their ability to provide essential care to patients who rely on the va system. the proposed exclusion also raises concerns about its impact on the patient-physician relationship, a core element of effective and high-quality medical care. family physicians are trained to engage in shared decision-making, where clinical recommendations are based on medical evidence and tailored to the individual needs and circumstances of each patient. by categorically excluding abortion and abortion counseling, this proposal impedes the ability of physicians to present the full range of medically appropriate options to their patients. the proposed rule states that abortion services would remain available when a physician certifies that the life of the pregnant individual would be endangered if the pregnancy were carried to term. while this exception is important, we encourage the va to allow physicians to exercise their clinical judgment across the full spectrum of patient health needs, rather than limiting their clinical decision-making to life-threatening circumstances. additionally, the proposed rule frames the 2022 policy change as a response to dobbs v. jackson women’s health organization, yet it does not address the implications of the supreme court’s decision should this proposed rule be finalized. specifically, the proposed rule fails to acknowledge that veterans in states with abortion bans may be denied access to medically necessary care in the absence of va support. by omitting this context, the rule overlooks the va’s responsibility to ensure timely and appropriate treatment for all veterans, regardless of location. accordingly, this proposal does not reflect current clinical practice or the diverse health needs of the veteran population. if finalized, patients may feel forced to seek care outside the va system, disrupting continuity of care and creating avoidable, and potentially harmful, barriers to medically appropriate treatment. such a policy risks compromising the trust, transparency, and quality of care veterans receive within the va system. we appreciate the opportunity to provide comments on this proposed rule. the aafp stands ready to collaborate with the va to ensure that its policies uphold the highest standards of clinical integrity and patient-centered care. for additional questions, please contact sahana chakravartti, regulatory specialist, at schakravartti@aafp.org. sincerely, steven furr, md, faafp american academy of physicians, board chair
VA-2025-VHA-0073-19876: on behalf of over 1.1 million momsrising members nationwide, we write to oppose the proposed rule titled “reproductive health services,” which would reinstate the exclusion of all abortion services from the medical benefits package for our veterans and their families. the proposed rule would restrict access to medical services in cases of rape, incest, and in cases of health endangerment of the pregnant person unless the life of the pregnant person is at risk. this policy would allow the department to willfully neglect the health of veterans and their families and deny them medically-necessary care unless they are on the brink of death. this is not the standard of care we should set for our country’s heroes. the department should be thanking our veterans by offering our heroes and their families the full spectrum of care available – which includes access to abortions. we have attached a letter that fully details our opposition to the proposed rule. ===== file 19876__1.pdf ===== september 2, 2025 uploaded to: https://www.regulations.gov/docket/va-2025-vha-0073 dr. steven l. lieberman acting under secretary for health department of veterans affairs 810 vermont avenue nw washington, d.c. 20420 comments on rin 2900-as31: reproductive health services proposed rule dear dr. lieberman: on behalf of over 1.1 million momsrising members nationwide, we submit these comments in opposition to the proposed rule titled “reproductive health services,” by the department of veterans affairs (“department” or “va”). we oppose the proposal to reinstate the exclusion of all abortion services from the medical benefits package for our veterans and their families. under the current policy, veterans and their families are guaranteed access to abortion services in cases of rape, incest, and in cases of health endangerment of the pregnant person. the proposed rule would restrict access to medical services in all these cases unless the life of the pregnant person is at risk. this policy would allow the department to willfully neglect the health of veterans and their families and deny them medically-necessary care unless they are on the brink of death. this is not the standard of care we should set for our country’s heroes. this proposed rule violates a core responsibility of va, which is to provide necessary care to veterans and to "promote, preserve, or restore the health" of their patients. but the va’s proposal does the exact opposite: it will set a confusing standard of care where providers can only provide the medically-necessary treatment in certain circumstances. out of fear of retaliation, service providers may offer a false prognosis, and the consequences could be fatal. our veterans fought for our fundamental freedoms. to strip them of their rights - including the ability to live a safe and healthy life - is an insult to all who have served. it is important to note that 6 in 10 women who access abortion are already moms. additionally, this proposal will have a particularly harmful impact on women veterans of color. as you know black women are disproportionately represented in the us military and in the veteran population. black women are three times more likely to experience a pregnancy-related death than white women and are more likely to experience preventable maternal death compared with white women. restrictions on abortion coverage - the effects of which fall hardest on people who already face unequal access to health care, including black women - interfere with a person’s right to make decisions about their health and well-being. we all deserve the freedom to control our own bodies, safely care for our families, and live with dignity. below are comments from our momsrising members who share the impact of the proposed policy reversal by the department: the young women of the armed forces get raped everyday and nothing is done about it. i was one of them years ago, the only reason i did not get pregnant was because i was on birth control. i had to have a hysterectomy for taking them too long. don't assume we are safe in the armed forces, women have to fight two battles: 1) being a woman and 2) not being raped. - barbara, armed forces veteran, georgia cutting abortion care when military sexual assault is rampant in these difficult times would be like throwing the baby out with the bathwater. kindly keep abortion services for my veteran sisters. - jim, us navy, vietnam veteran, california the department should be thanking our veterans by offering our heroes and their families the full spectrum of care available – which includes access to abortions. leaving veterans who have been sexually assaulted, veterans who would suffer severe health consequences for carrying a pregnancy to term, or any veteran in need of an abortion without the care they need is not how we should honor their service. for these reasons, we strongly oppose the proposed rule to restrict reproductive healthcare for our veterans. sincerely, tina sherman national director for maternal justice momsrising together & momsrising education fund gina arias, rn, mph campaign director for maternal mental health momsrising together & momsrising education fund

nonprofit agency and while we partner with many government and non-government agencies, we are a completely independent nonprofit. as a recovery-focused organization, cvlc primarily, but not exclusively, serves clients through a medical-legal partnership model in which we partner with veterans administration hospitals (“the va”) and other connected providers to provide holistic support for veterans alongside their clinicians to secure housing and access to healthcare and income benefits. our mission is to empower, support, and improve the lives of connecticut veterans by providing free legal assistance to help them overcome legal barriers to housing, healthcare, income, and recovery. through our work, we have represented many veterans who became pregnant in service as a result of rape and who were forced to carry the pregnancy to term. va did not provide abortion or abortion counseling prior to 2022, and our clients who were pregnant due to sexual assault during that time period suffered both mentally and physically because of those pregnancies it is for this reason that we issue comment on this proposed rule, urging va to provide abortion care 2 and counseling in accordance with federal law and not to promulgate the proposed exclusion of healthcare services. ii. existing federal law mandates that abortion may be used in cases of rape, incest, and the welfare of the mother. the hyde amendment was enacted september 30, 1976. the law states that federal funds could not generally be used to pay for an abortion, but in all versions of the amendment passed since 1994, provides exceptions for the life of the mother and when the pregnancy results from rape or incest.1 since the supreme court overturned roe v. wade, states have been able draft state-specific abortion laws that may not include exceptions for the life of the mother or for rape or incest. the hyde amendment, however, has not been modified to remove these exceptions.2 as the left to deal with pregnancies resulting from sexual assault or incest, incidents that are traumatic unto themselves without the addition of a pregnancy. in states where abortion is illegal, women amendment. should a doctor order that a woman receive an abortion due to hemorrhage, a severe birth defect, or a miscarriage, that order should be self- evident. if a doctor must certify that this abortion would save the life of the mother, it will have a chilling effect on doctors practicing medicine and providing the best care possible for their patients. 1 see lieu, edward and shen, wen, the
