VA-2025-VHA-0073-19950: please see the attached document for the complete comments from the american medical association. ===== file 19950__1.pdf ===== september 2, 2025 the honorable douglas collins secretary u.s. department of veterans affairs 810 vermont avenue, nw washington, dc 20420 re: rin 2900-as31: reproductive health services dear secretary collins: on behalf of the physician and medical student members of the american medical association (ama), i appreciate the opportunity to offer our comments to the department of veterans affairs (va) on the proposal to reinstate the full exclusion of coverage for abortions and abortion counseling for the va medical benefits package and the civilian health and medical program of the department of veterans affairs (champva).1 the ama strongly supports preserving access to evidence-based reproductive health care services, including abortion, and supports the basic medical principle that clinical assessments, such as the safety of the pregnant patient and appropriate course of treatment, are determinations to be made only by physicians with their patients. in alignment with these principles, the ama asks that the va reconsider its proposed changes to the va and champva reproductive health services benefits and retain existing exceptions that permit abortion under certain, limited circumstances. under 38 u.s.c. 1710(a)(1) through (3), the va is authorized to furnish hospital care and medical services that the secretary determines to be needed through the va’s medical benefits package. abortion care has long been excluded from va benefits except, prior to 2022, when necessary to preserve the life of the pregnant woman. in 2022, the va revised regulations to permit abortion if the life or health of the pregnant beneficiary would be endangered if the pregnancy were carried to term or if the pregnancy was the result of rape or incest. the proposed rule would revert coverage to pre-2022 levels to exclude abortion and abortion counseling and to permit abortion under champva only when a physician certifies that the life of the mother would be endangered if the fetus was carried to term. the preamble also states that the exclusion of abortion would not apply in life-threatening circumstances under the va benefits package; however, this is not reflected in the proposed revisions to § 17.38. the shift to allow abortion only when necessary to save the life, but not the health, of the mother is deeply concerning and fails to reflect the nature of pregnancy complications. serious and emergent conditions during pregnancy may not be immediately life-threatening but still pose significant risks to patients’ health. conditions such as severe preeclampsia, severe kidney disease, and complications from prelabor rupture of membranes can often be resolved, prior to fetal viability, by terminating the pregnancy before a patient faces a significant risk of death but, if left untreated, can rapidly become life-threatening with little or no warning. further, there is no bright line in medicine to determine when a condition goes from endangering a patient’s health to jeopardizing her life. reflecting this reality, physicians are trained to intervene to prevent the deterioration of a patient’s condition before it becomes life-threatening. but by 1 https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/08/04/2025-14687/reproductive-health-services. the honorable douglas collins september 2, 2025 page 2 eliminating the “health” exception, the proposed rule would tie the hands of physicians caring for veterans and their families. instead of following well-established medical guidelines and medical ethics, physicians will be forced to delay appropriate, stabilizing care until the patient’s life is in jeopardy, subjecting patients to avoidable risk and needless suffering. we strongly urge the va to retain the exceptions currently recognized in both § 17.38 and § 17.272. we are also concerned by the proposal to exclude abortion counseling. counseling is a vital part of the informed decision-making process, and the ama believes that it is essential for physicians to offer clear, nonjudgmental, and medically accurate information to their patients, especially when facing difficult and personal decisions about abortion. denying veterans and their families the ability to receive critical information about their health and the risks and benefits of different courses of action contradicts established medical ethics that prioritize patient autonomy and informed consent. veterans, like all patients, deserve the opportunity to receive unbiased, comprehensive counseling on all their reproductive health care options, including, when appropriate, the termination of pregnancy. the removal of counseling would severely limit the ability of physicians to support patients in making fully informed decisions about their health and their families, and we ask the va to maintain this coverage. the termination of pregnancy is a medical matter between the patient and the physician, subject to the physician’s clinical judgment, the patient’s informed consent, and the ability to perform the procedure safely. pregnancy complications can develop and worsen quickly, and it is essential that physicians be able to exercise their clinical judgment to intervene in accordance with established medical guidelines to avert needless suffering and harm. we strongly urge the va to retain its current coverage of abortion, as well as abortion counseling, to ensure that pregnant veterans and their families receive the highest standard of care. we greatly appreciate your consideration of our comments and requests. please reach out to me directly at 312-464-5288 or john.whyte@ama-assn.org if you have questions or need further information. sincerely, john whyte, md, mph

VA-2025-VHA-0073-20040: the washington state coalition against domestic violence (wscadv) writes to express our strong opposition to the department of veterans affairs’ proposed rule on reproductive health services. we also write in full support of the public comment submitted by the national alliance to end sexual violence (naesv) and the 25 undersigned national and state organizations. as washington state’s leading voice advocating for survivors of domestic violence and sexual assault, wscadv is deeply concerned that the proposed rule would roll back critical reproductive healthcare access for veterans and their families—particularly those who have experienced sexual and domestic violence. the va’s proposal to reinstate pre-2022 exclusions on abortion and abortion counseling would deny essential care to survivors, including in cases of rape, incest, or threats to the life or health of the pregnant person. veterans in washington state and across the country deserve access to comprehensive, trauma-informed healthcare. this includes reproductive healthcare that recognizes the unique needs of survivors of military sexual trauma (mst), intimate partner violence, and other forms of gender-based violence. the va’s own data and national research have consistently shown that women veterans experience sexual violence at disproportionately high rates, and that mst is associated with serious long-term health consequences including ptsd, depression, and substance use disorders. restricting access to abortion and abortion counseling not only undermines bodily autonomy—it also increases the risk of continued abuse and trauma. survivors must be empowered to make decisions about their own health and futures, especially when those decisions are shaped by experiences of violence. the va’s healthcare system must be a place of safety, healing, and support—not one that retraumatizes survivors by denying them care. we urge the department to reject the proposed rule and maintain the protections established in the 2022 interim final rule and the 2024 final rule. wscadv stands with naesv and other advocates in calling for the va to uphold its commitment to the health and dignity of all veterans and their families.

VA-2025-VHA-0073-20061: we write today to comment on the department of veterans affairs’ (va) proposed rule, rin: 2900-as31, published in the federal register on august 4, 2025, to reinstate a near-total ban on abortions and abortion counseling from va’s medical benefits package. this incredibly dangerous and reckless rule change will take away essential health care for veterans and beneficiaries of the civilian health and medical program of the department of veterans affairs (champva). for the past three years, these patients have been able to obtain comprehensive pregnancy counseling, including information about abortion services, and abortion care in cases of rape, incest, or life or health endangerment. this proposed rule seriously calls into question whether the department is putting political allegiances and culture wars ahead of its sacred obligation to deliver quality, life-saving health care to veterans, including the more than 462,000 women veterans of reproductive age enrolled in va health care. please see attachment to view our full comment letter. ===== file 20061__1.pdf ===== september 2, 2025 steven l. lieberman, md acting under secretary for health department of veterans affairs 810 vermont avenue nw washington, dc 20420 dear dr. lieberman, we write today to comment on the department of veterans affairs’ (va) proposed rule, rin: 2900-as31, published in the federal register on august 4, 2025, to reinstate a near-total ban on abortions and abortion counseling from va’s medical benefits package. this incredibly dangerous and reckless rule change will take away essential health care for veterans and beneficiaries of the civilian health and medical program of the department of veterans affairs (champva). for the past three years, these patients have been able to obtain comprehensive pregnancy counseling, including information about abortion services, and abortion care in cases of rape, incest, or life or health endangerment. this proposed rule seriously calls into question whether the department is putting political allegiances and culture wars ahead of its sacred obligation to deliver quality, life-saving health care to veterans, including the more than 462,000 women veterans of reproductive age enrolled in va health care. we reject this rule’s premise that only providing a carveout for abortions in cases of life endangerment is adequate for providing “needed” health care for veterans. evidence has shown that extreme abortion bans, like the ban this rule would create, cause chaos and confusion for providers, putting them in the impossible position of navigating laws that don’t allow them to deliver the appropriate standard of care to ailing patients. worse, such a ban would also be extremely dangerous to the health and wellbeing of veterans. as we have seen in states with extreme abortion bans, even those with “life exceptions” in place, patients have faced severe health complications and even death in cases when providers did not know if the patient’s life was endangered enough to be covered under this exception. additionally, though this proposed rule claims “[n]o state law prohibits treatment for ectopic pregnancies or miscarriages to save the life of a mother,” there are numerous cases of providers nationwide being unable to provide care for women with ectopic pregnancies or experiencing miscarriages, due to restrictive, ambiguous laws. as such, this rule will now require va providers to make the impossible determination of whether a veteran is close enough to death to be covered under the “threat to life” exception before providing an abortion. va’s proposed rule presupposes that a blanket prohibition and a narrow, undefined exception will be sufficient to ensure va can provide “needed” care to veterans and that “the lives of pregnant women will continue to be protected…” instead of trusting veterans and their providers to decide on a path forward that actually meets patients’ needs and protects their lives. this is no way to treat our veterans, or va providers. beyond the ban on abortion care, the prohibition on abortion counseling in this proposed rule also endangers va’s ability to provide appropriate care to veterans. regardless of the reason a veteran chooses or needs to seek abortion care, they must be allowed to discuss all their health care options openly and honestly with their provider. in removing va providers’ ability to provide comprehensive, evidence-based pregnancy counseling, including information about abortion services, in this proposed rule, the department is unnecessarily and detrimentally allowing the government to interfere with health care decisions that should be between a veteran and their provider. in putting forth this proposed rule, va has decided that its political judgement and legal analysis should supplant medical care decisions that are best made by providers and the patients in their care, even in life and death situations. further, despite va’s argument that previous eligibility requirements for abortion care and counseling at the department – as put in place under the biden administration’s september 9, 2022, interim final rule – were contradictory to “decades of federal policy against forced taxpayer funding for abortion,” the biden-era rule brought va more in line with abortion coverage in other federal programs. most federally funded health programs – including those covered under the hyde amendment – have carveouts for abortions in cases of rape, incest, or life endangerment. va’s rule will lead to an inequity for veterans and champva beneficiaries when compared to their civilian counterparts, making their access to abortion care more limited than those who use almost any other federally funded health care program. this proposed rule also claims the biden-era rule was an act of overreach, “creating a purported federal entitlement to abortion for veterans where none had existed before and without regard to state law.” in reality, the department has previously issued a regulation (38 cfr 17.419) confirming the ability of va providers to practice their health care profession consistent with the scope of their va employment, regardless of any state license, registration, certification, or other requirements that unduly interfere with their practice. additionally, the justice department issued an opinion after the release of the biden-era rule, citing the supremacy clause of the u.s. constitution and its applicability to the biden rule: “[s]tates may not impose criminal or civil liability on va employees…who provide or facilitate abortions or related services in a manner authorized by federal law, including va’s rule.” given the applicability of va’s own regulations and the supremacy clause of the u.s. constitution, we fail to see how the department can reject the biden-era rule on the premise of “overreach.” finally, we find the department’s claim that “abortion is not a ‘needed’ service for veterans” to be insulting and ignorant. veterans of reproductive age have high rates of chronic health conditions – many of which may be service connected, including post-traumatic stress disorder (ptsd), severe hypertension, and renal disease – that can increase the risks associated with a pregnancy. if a provider determines these conditions or others make an abortion necessary to preserve a veteran or champva beneficiary’s health, access to abortion should be considered essential health care. in addition, veterans who are forced to carry to term pregnancies resulting from rape or incest are at risk of long-lasting psychological conditions and traumatic stress, making abortion access for these veterans needed for protecting their health. it is also vital given the high incidence of military sexual trauma in the armed forces, and the number of veterans who already suffer from ptsd or other mental health conditions. the concerns we raise about this cruel proposal to roll back essential health care for veterans are not ours alone – they are shared by veterans and their families nationwide. a survey conducted by iraq and afghanistan veterans of america after the u.s. supreme court’s dobbs v. jackson women’s health organization decision found more than two-thirds of their members surveyed supported both va and the department of defense stepping in to ensure veterans, servicemembers, and their families have access to the reproductive care they need. since the dobbs decision, more than half of women veterans and champva beneficiaries of reproductive age live in states that have enacted abortion bans or restrictions. should their health be in jeopardy due to a pregnancy, or if they are raped, this rule will leave them with nowhere to turn. to finalize this rule will be a failure for our veterans, and we urge the department to reconsider. thank you for your consideration of this comment. sincerely, richard blumenthal united states senator mark takano member of congress charles e. schumer united states senator hakeem jeffries member of congress VA-2025-VHA-0073-20063: see attached file(s) ===== file 20063__1.pdf ===== robert vinson brannum rbrannum@robertbrannum.com september 2, 2025 the honorable douglas collins secretary department of veterans affairs washington, dc re: proposed rule dear mr secretary, as printed in the federal register, "the department of veterans affairs (va) is proposing to reinstate the full exclusion on abortions and abortion counseling from the medical benefits package, which was removed in 2022. before that time, this exclusion had been firmly in place since the medical benefits package was first established in 1999. va is also proposing to reinstate the exclusions on abortion and abortion counseling for civilian health and medical program of the department of veterans affairs (champva) that were removed in 2022. we take this action to ensure that va provides only needed medical services to our nation's heroes and their families." i am a service-connected disabled veteran. i am a man. i strongly oppose this proposed rule. it is clearly and demonstrably discriminatory. further, i join those who view abortion as essential care which should be veterans in cases of rape, incest, or when pregnancy endangered a veteran's health or life. let me be clear and precise, the right to an abortion is a right to be included in health care. this proposed rule is offensive to justice, decency, and a blatant disregard for the health of veterans who need this medical service. this rule hinders the availability of veterans to receive full and complete medical treatment. this proposed rule is dishonest and should not be affirmed.

introduction the u.s. department of veteran’s affairs (va) amended its medical benefits package on september 9, 2022 to permit pregnant beneficiaries of the veterans and civilian health and medical program of the department of veterans affairs (champva) to access abortion services when the life or the health of the pregnant veteran would be endangered if the pregnancy were carried to term, or if the pregnancy resulted from an act of rape or incest. champva regulations were also changed in 2022 to permit abortion counseling, as a part of a comprehensive counseling of pregnancy options, for veterans, spouses, and dependents to allow patients to make informed decisions about their care. this brought veteran and champva care in line with tricare, which already had these provisions for abortion care and abortion counseling.1 the new york state department of health and the department of veterans services (the departments) write to express their joint opposition to the proposed rule. impacts of the proposed rule the va now proposes rule rin 2900-as31, which would reinstate pre-2022 full exclusions on abortions and abortion counseling, claiming this will "ensure that va provides only needed medical services to our nation's heroes and their families." the number of impacted veterans and family members is substantial. it is estimated that in the united states, there are more than two-million-woman veterans2 and thousands of transgender men and non-binary veterans3 who would be eligible for abortion care. there are 700,000 family members eligible for champva that would also be impacted.4 further, va secretary doug collins has stated repeatedly that his top priority is the prevention of veteran suicide. this priority is undermined with this proposed regulatory change. in december 2022, for instance, the peer-reviewed journal jama psychiatry published a longitudinal study verifying that restricting abortion access is linked to increased suicide risk for women of reproductive age.5 thus, if secretary collins truly wishes to prioritize the prevention of veteran suicide, then abortion care and counseling is indeed scientifically proven to be a "needed medical services to our nation's heroes and their families."6 it is important to note that abortion care and counseling is recognized as medical care by leading medical bodies, including the american college of obstetricians and gynecologists. removing the abortion care and counseling provision for veterans and champva would create confusion among veterans and their families and create uneven access to care based on where in the country veterans live. access to care for those who have given so much to our country should not be dependent on state lines; all veterans deserve access to quality, affordable medical care. rape provision the current medical benefits package excludes abortions, except in cases of rape and incest and health of the pregnant person. women veterans experiencing homelessness are among the most at-risk populations for sexual assault. furthermore, during their service one in three female veterans report experiencing sexual assault.7 when examining female veterans who are unhoused, up to 40% have experienced military sexual trauma.8 additionally, female veterans experienced unsheltered homelessness at a higher rate than sheltered homelessness (12% vs 9%), meaning they are more likely to spend time on the street and not in a shelter.9 because these female veterans experiencing homelessness have an increased risk that they become victims of sexual violence,10 this would mean they could need abortion care under the current medical regulations, but would be turned away from care if these medical regulations were changed. health of the pregnant person provision there are inherent risks to military family and spouses, as well as female veterans if abortion access is prohibited and pregnancies are forced to progress: the risk to the health of the pregnant person. pregnancies have inherent risks, with 700 people dying each year in the us from pregnancy-related conditions and 50,000 people having short- or long-term health complications from their pregnancy or birth.11 this rule could impede treatment for ectopic pregnancy, for example. these pregnancies are never viable and can result in severe complications, including death, if not treated urgently. if veterans and champva recipients are denied abortion care services when the life or the health of the pregnant person would be endangered if the pregnancy were carried to term, this would result in severe complications or death. even a delay in seeking care can be devastating. the change in medical regulations puts veterans and their dependents at risk. conclusion abortion care is a critical component of healthcare.12,13,14 both the american college of obstetricians and gynecologists and the society of maternal-fetal medicine oppose policies that limit abortion access and/or a healthcare providers ability to counsel patients.13,14 the change in these medical regulations stand in stark contrast to these recommendations. many veterans fought for years to eliminate these long-standing barriers at veterans health administration facilities. to have them reinstated now is a step backward. veterans health administration is the largest integrated healthcare network in the nation, and should prioritize the provision of this critical counseling and care. the new york state department of health and the new york state department of veterans services appreciates va’s consideration of our comments on this proposed rule and urges the agency to keep the medical benefits package as it is currently and not revert back to where they were before september 8, 2022. if changes are made, it will cause undue harm to the veterans and families of veterans on champva across the country. if you require additional information about the issues raised in these comments, please contact associate commissioner of governmental and external affairs alyssa derosa, at alyssa.derosa@health.ny.gov. references: federal register, volume 87 issue 174 (friday, VA-2025-VHA-0073-20479: please find attached comment from dav (disabled american veterans). ===== file 20479__1.pdf ===== september 3, 2025 director, office of regulation policy and management (00reg) department of veterans affairs, 810 vermont avenue, nw, room 1064 washington, dc 20420 re: proposed rule on reproductive health services (rin 2900-as31) fr document 2025-14687 citation: 90 fr 36415 dav (disabled american veterans) is pleased to respond to the department of veterans affairs (va) notice of the proposed rule on reproductive health services, as published in the federal register on august 4, 2025. summary and background: the va is proposing to significantly limit access to abortion services and abortion counseling in its medical benefits package by reverting applicable regulations (38 cfr 17.38 and 17.272) to their pre-2022 iteration, which only included an exception for abortions to be provided by va or paid for through the civilian health and medical program of the department of veterans affairs (champva) if the life of the pregnant woman was endangered. dav opposes this rule. in september 2022, following the supreme court’s issuance of the dobbs v. jackson women's health organization, va issued an interim final rule (ifr) (87 fr 55287, september 9, 2022) that expanded the instances in which abortions could be performed or paid for to include abortions for women when the pregnancy was the result of rape or incest, or because the pregnant woman’s health would be endangered if the pregnancy were carried to term. the 2022 ifr also removed the exclusion of abortion counseling for va health care providers as well as champva providers. the newly proposed rule would reinstate the prior exclusion on abortion coverage, only allowing an exception when the life of the pregnant woman would be endangered. it would also exclude all abortion counseling services by va and through champva. comments dav is a congressionally chartered and va-accredited veterans service organization (vso) with nearly a million veteran members, all of whom have been disabled, injured or made ill during wartime service. we are dedicated to ensuring that veterans, their families, caregivers, 2 and survivors can access the full range of benefits and services available to them, to include high-quality, comprehensive health care and specialized and gender-specific programs for both men and women. for women veterans specifically, we advocate to ensure access to comprehensive services to meet their unique health care needs, including reproductive care services, inclusive of counseling and psychological services related to combat exposure, intimate partner violence or sexual trauma. since the creation of va’s modern medical benefits package in 1999, as required by the veterans’ health care eligibility reform act of 1996 (public law 104-262), until the issuance of the ifr in september 2022, va has generally had a prohibition against providing or paying for abortion services and abortion counseling, allowing an exception only when the life of the pregnant woman would be endangered. however, va’s long held policy on abortion has not been consistent with other federal health care programs that are generally bound by the hyde amendment, an amendment to federal appropriations bills that prohibits the use of federal funds for abortions. since 1993, the hyde amendment has included exceptions for instances of rape and incest, or when the life of the pregnant woman is in danger. these exceptions have applied to most federal health care and insurance programs, including the department of defense (dod), federal bureau of prisons, federal employee health benefits, medicaid, indian health service and others. however, the proposed rule would not include the exceptions for rape or incest, consistent with the longstanding hyde amendment. in practice, this could mean a female service member who was raped prior to transitioning out of military service, and who learns she is pregnant after enrolling in the va health care system, would not be covered by va to have an abortion. had she still been on active duty, dod would have paid or performed the abortion; if she worked for va, her federal employee health insurance would have paid for the abortion; and even if she was serving time in a federal prison, her abortion would have been covered. however, as an enrollee in the va health care system, she would not have been covered even for an abortion resulting from rape. we also note that earlier this year on january 25, the president issued an executive order called “enforcing the hyde amendment” which it described it as “…established, commonsense policy…” and called for federal policy to be “…consistent with the hyde amendment…” however, as discussed above, the proposed rule is not consistent with the hyde amendment. we recognize that abortion is a deeply sensitive issue that elicits strong views by americans from different backgrounds and across the political spectrum. while public debate will continue, dav’s responsibility is to ensure that policy decisions remain centered on the health, safety, and well-being of our nation’s wartime service-disabled veterans. consistent with our constitution, bylaws and adopted resolutions, we believe that medical services available to veterans through the va medical benefits package should not be reduced or taken away as a result of regulatory or legislative changes. any policy changes proposed must put veterans’ health and safety first—especially for women veterans who may face complex reproductive health challenges requiring timely, expert care. va must continue expanding 3 gender-specific and comprehensive services to meet the needs of the growing women veteran population. for all of the aforementioned reasons, dav opposes the proposed rule. whenever va pursues changes to its medical benefits package, it must work closely with veterans and veteran stakeholders in developing such changes, and must provide clear and consistent guidance to veterans, providers, and congress to ensure new or modified policies are applied safely across the system. stakeholders should work together, as we have on many past issues, to preserve va’s capacity to deliver high-quality, comprehensive care. dav will continue to advocate for equitable, timely access to safe, high-quality care for all veterans. we remain committed to working together with congress, va, and our vso partners to strengthen and sustain the va health care system so that va remains the primary provider and coordinator of health care for enrolled veterans. sincerely, joy j. ilem national legislative director

evidence, and to ensure that the voices, interests, and freedoms of americans, and especially of small businesses, are fully represented in the regulatory process and debates. finally, we work to ensure that regulatory proposals address real problems, that the proposals serve to ameliorate those problems, and, perhaps most importantly, that those proposals do not, in fact, make public policy problems worse. introduction the cpac foundation’s center for regulatory freedom (crf) submits these comments not only in support of the department of veterans affairs’ proposed rule to reinstate the exclusion of abortion and abortion counseling services, but as part of our broader mission to defend religious freedom and conscience protections across the federal regulatory landscape. this rule offers a 2 rare and commendable course correction—one that rebukes an alarming trend of bureaucratic hostility toward americans of faith that accelerated during the biden administration. crf has long raised alarms over this ideological overreach, which has repeatedly threatened the foundational constitutional liberties of health professionals, students, veterans, and everyday citizens. in recent years, crf and its allies have filed numerous public comments across federal agencies—documenting a consistent and deliberate effort by the biden administration to subvert religious liberty through executive fiat. at the department of health and human services, for example, the administration sought to gut the trump-era conscience protections that shield medical professionals from participating in abortion and gender-transition procedures. we condemned this as not only unlawful but unconstitutional, emphasizing that rights of conscience are “first liberty principles” that cannot be brushed aside by shifting political winds. the pattern has repeated itself across agencies. at the equal employment opportunity commission, the administration reinterpreted the bipartisan pregnant workers fairness act to include abortion access—explicitly defying congressional intent. at the department of education, it attempted to dismantle the free inquiry rule, which had protected religious student organizations from discrimination based on their faith-based membership or leadership standards. through these actions, the administration exhibited a troubling disregard for the first amendment, using regulatory instruments to marginalize religious perspectives under the guise of inclusion and access. crf has consistently responded by reminding agencies that conscience rights are not obstacles to governance—they are constitutional guarantees that predate and supersede administrative policy. in our comments to hhs and doe, we underscored that the administrative procedure act does not empower agencies to invent policy contrary to statute or to manipulate cost-benefit analysis to sidestep constitutional restraints. when religious liberty is subordinated to ideology, regulatory legitimacy crumbles. our defense of these rights is not partisan—it is principled, grounded in the rule of law, and rooted in the belief that no american should be compelled to violate their deeply held beliefs to participate in civil society or serve their country. in this context, the va’s current proposal to reverse the 2022 abortion policy is more than a welcome shift—it is a vital restoration of legal and moral order. it honors the conscience rights of medical providers and veterans alike, realigns va health services with clear statutory limits, and affirms that the federal government does not have a mandate to impose ideological conformity through regulatory fiat. this proposed rule is precisely the kind of governance crf has long advocated: restrained, constitutional, and respectful of the diverse moral convictions of the american people. executive summary the cpac foundation’s center for regulatory freedom (crf) strongly supports the department of veterans affairs’ proposed rule to reinstate the exclusion of abortion and abortion counseling from the va medical benefits package and the champva program. this rule marks a crucial and overdue return to legal clarity, medical integrity, and constitutional order. the 2022 interim final rule (ifr), imposed under the biden administration, constituted an unlawful and ideologically motivated departure from decades of precedent. it redefined abortion as a “needed” medical service—without statutory basis and in direct conflict with the veterans 3 health care act of 1992, the hyde amendment, and 38 u.s.c. §1710. the administration’s claims of urgent post-dobbs demand were unfounded, with actual procedures performed under the policy totaling far below projections. more egregiously, the 2022 ifr trampled on the religious freedom and conscience rights of va clinicians, chaplains, and staff. by forcing participation in or support for abortion procedures, it violated federal protections such as the religious freedom restoration act (rfra), the church amendments, and the weldon amendment. the rule also extended this flawed policy to family members and caregivers under champva, despite a clear lack of legal authority to do so. the proposed rollback corrects these abuses. it restores the va to its proper mission—providing truly needed care to veterans—while respecting congressional intent, longstanding agency policy, and the deeply held beliefs of service providers and taxpayers. it preserves necessary emergency care exceptions while eliminating elective abortion as a mischaracterized “health care benefit.” the crf urges the department to finalize this rule without delay and views it as a necessary reassertion of regulatory discipline and constitutional restraint. this is a victory not only for veterans, but for the rule of law, religious liberty, and the integrity of federal governance. i. history: the biden administration, abortion, religious freedom and matters of conscience during its tenure, the biden administration pursued an expansive, ideologically driven campaign to normalize taxpayer-funded abortion access across all facets of the federal government. utilizing a “whole of government” strategy, the administration worked to embed pro-abortion mandates across multiple federal agencies, while simultaneously undermining decades of bipartisan protections for religious conscience and first amendment freedoms. this radical policy orientation became evident through regulatory actions across the department of veterans affairs (va), the department of health and human services (hhs), the equal employment opportunity commission (eeoc), and the department of education (doe). through each of these, the administration pushed federal agencies far beyond their statutory authority, effectively weaponizing the administrative state to advance a deeply partisan social agenda. although the va has now proposed to reverse course and restore long-standing prohibitions against abortion and abortion counseling, a review of the biden administration’s record is critical to understanding why this reversal is necessary—and how dangerous its original policy trajectory was. a coordinated, multi-agency strategy to normalize abortion access from the outset, the biden administration treated abortion access not as a limited and controversial procedure subject to state law or legislative control, but as a universal entitlement that could be imposed by executive decree. it did so through a coordinated network of agency rulemakings and policy reinterpretations designed to bypass congress and nullify decades of statutory and constitutional precedent. 4 at the va, the administration removed long-standing prohibitions against abortion and abortion counseling from the va medical benefits package and the champva program in september 2022. these prohibitions had existed since 1999 and were consistent with 38 u.s.c. § 1710, which authorized only “needed” medical care—not elective abortions. the administration’s justification for the change was the dobbs decision, yet its own estimates of demand proved wildly inflated. despite projecting over 1,000 annual abortion procedures, actual numbers remained closer to 100. at hhs, the administration rescinded the trump-era 2019 conscience rule, which had restored robust protections for medical professionals who objected to participating in abortion and gender-transition procedures. by repealing these protections, the administration effectively forced religious doctors and nurses to violate their conscience or leave their profession. at the eeoc, the administration issued a rule interpreting the bipartisan pregnant workers fairness act (pwfa) to require employers to accommodate abortion—a position congress explicitly rejected. lawmakers from both parties stated unequivocally that the pwfa was intended to protect pregnant women in the workplace, not to promote or subsidize abortion. at the department of education, the administration proposed rescinding the free inquiry rule, which had safeguarded the rights of faith-based student organizations to operate according to their beliefs. this move, framed as a cost-benefit adjustment, was in reality an assault on the free exercise and free association rights of religious students across the country. these efforts were not isolated incidents. they formed a cohesive strategy to impose a progressive ideological framework across every corner of the federal government—one that redefined abortion as a protected right, and religious liberty as an obstacle to be removed. bypassing congress, subverting the constitution a hallmark of the biden administration’s approach was its disregard for the legislative process. rather than working with congress to amend laws, it systematically exploited ambiguities in existing statutes or fabricated them where none existed. this was evident in its redefinition of what constitutes “needed” medical care at the va, or what qualifies as a “related medical condition” under the pwfa. nowhere was this clearer than at the va. for over two decades, the va interpreted its statutory authority under 38 u.s.c. § 1710 as not authorizing abortion. this interpretation was consistent, bipartisan, and uncontroversial—until the biden administration unilaterally declared otherwise in 2022. in doing so, it ignored the express language of the veterans health care act of 1992, which specifically excluded abortions, and it claimed new authority without congressional approval. the administration also disregarded the constitution’s protections for religious liberty. across multiple agencies, it proposed or finalized rules that would compel religious organizations and individuals to violate their beliefs. at hhs, it narrowed the definition of who qualifies for conscience protections. at the eeoc, it sought to force faith-based employers to accommodate abortions. at doe, it tried to strip student religious groups of recognition and access. 5 distorting health policy to serve ideological ends the administration’s justification for these sweeping changes often rested on the redefinition of abortion as “health care.” this rhetorical sleight of hand allowed agencies to treat abortion as a standard medical procedure, on par with childbirth or cancer treatment—despite abortion’s moral, ethical, and political distinctiveness. this was most apparent in the va’s 2022 interim final rule. despite the absence of any congressional mandate or meaningful evidence of demand, the administration insisted that abortion had become a “needed” service for veterans in the wake of dobbs. this assertion was not only unsupported by the data—it directly contradicted the intent of the law, which had long drawn a bright line between medical care and elective abortion. similarly, at the eeoc, the administration twisted the plain language of the pwfa—crafted to protect pregnant women and their unborn children—to include accommodations for abortion. this was not a matter of ambiguous statutory interpretation. it was a deliberate effort to flip the legislative purpose on its head, and to use a bipartisan law as a trojan horse for a deeply divisive policy agenda. attacks on religious freedom were deliberate, not accidental in each of these actions, the biden administration subordinated religious liberty to its abortion agenda. conscience rights were treated as negotiable; constitutional protections were seen as inconveniences. faith-based objections were neither accommodated nor tolerated—they were steamrolled. the rescission of the hhs conscience rule erased protections that had safeguarded religious doctors and nurses since 2008. the administration’s stated rationale was that the rule was overly broad—but its real purpose was to eliminate any meaningful ability for religious health professionals to abstain from participating in procedures they found morally objectionable. the attempted reinterpretation of the pwfa ignored explicit statements from lawmakers like sen. bill cassidy and sen. bob casey, who had affirmed that abortion would not be included under the law. the eeoc’s regulation disregarded this legislative history and acted as if those statements had never been made. the proposed rollback of the free inquiry rule at doe was couched in bureaucratic language about “cost-benefit analysis,” but its real effect would have been to strip protections for religious student groups, opening the door for universities to deny them recognition based on their beliefs. taken together, these actions were not mistakes. they reflected a deliberate effort to impose a uniform moral framework that excluded—and often punished—religious dissent. ii. va’s proposed rule: a return to common sense and constitutional order the va’s current proposed rule—to restore the abortion exclusions that were in place before september 2022—is a welcome and necessary correction. it aligns the department’s medical benefits package with its statutory authority, longstanding agency precedent, and the will of the american people. 6 the 2022 rule was an outlier—a reckless policy change made in response to a supreme court decision that returned abortion policymaking to the states. rather than respecting that decision, the biden administration used it as an excuse to expand federal abortion access and override state law. the proposed rollback restores the va to its proper role: a provider of needed medical care for veterans, not a tool for ideological experimentation. it also reaffirms the principle that major changes in social policy should come from congress—not from unelected bureaucrats. the cpac foundation's center for regulatory freedom strongly supports the department of veterans affairs' (va) proposed rule to restore the exclusions on abortion and abortion counseling in the va medical benefits package and the champva program. this proposal is not only legally sound and medically responsible, but it also corrects one of the most egregious abuses of regulatory authority undertaken during the biden administration: the weaponization of the va to promote a radical, pro-abortion agenda at the expense of religious liberty, conscience rights, and the statutory limits set by congress. for over two decades, the va properly interpreted its statutory authority under 38 u.s.c. §1710 to exclude abortion and abortion counseling from its health care services. the 2022 interim final rule (ifr), issued in the wake of the supreme court’s dobbs decision, represented a sharp and unlawful break from that longstanding precedent. it declared elective abortion a "needed" medical service, without statutory support, in open defiance of congressional intent and agency precedent. the result was a dangerous and ideologically driven overreach that placed the va in direct conflict with state laws, undermined trust in the agency, and trampled the conscience rights of health care providers and taxpayers alike. the current proposed rule reverses this misstep and restores integrity to the va health care system. correcting regulatory overreach and legal error va's authority to provide care under §1710 has always been constrained by the requirement that services must be "needed." for decades, successive administrations understood that elective abortion did not meet this standard. the 1992 veterans health care act specifically excluded abortion from va reproductive health services, and until 2022, that exclusion was upheld in both regulation and practice. the 2022 ifr falsely claimed that dobbs created an urgent demand for abortion access within the va system. in reality, the projected surge in demand never materialized. va data show that fewer than 150 abortions were performed annually under the 2022 policy—far below the projected 1,000+. this data confirms what the law already made clear: abortion is not a necessary medical service for veterans, nor is it appropriate for taxpayer funding. the current proposal brings va policy back into alignment with the law and reflects the actual medical needs of veterans. more importantly, it restores the original statutory interpretation of "needed" care and affirms that the agency must act within its legal boundaries. 7 restoring conscience rights and religious liberty the biden-era policy change did more than violate legal norms—it imposed real and immediate harms on religious health care providers within the va system. by classifying abortion as a "needed" service, the administration effectively compelled va clinicians, chaplains, and support staff to participate in, refer for, or otherwise facilitate abortion procedures in violation of their deeply held beliefs. this action disregarded the rights of conscience protected under federal law, including the religious freedom restoration act (rfra) and statutory conscience provisions like the church amendments and the weldon amendment. worse still, the administration's policy was implemented without meaningful accommodations for those whose religious beliefs prohibit participation in abortion. the proposed rule recognizes and corrects this constitutional error. it removes va employees from the impossible position of choosing between their jobs and their faith. it restores a culture of respect and pluralism within va facilities, where all medical personnel—regardless of their beliefs—can serve veterans without violating their conscience. aligning with congressional intent and public sentiment congress has consistently drawn a clear line between health care and abortion. federal programs such as medicaid, tricare, and the federal employees health benefits program all prohibit funding for elective abortions. the hyde amendment, in place since 1976, reflects the will of the american people that taxpayer dollars should not be used to pay for abortion. the 2022 ifr arrogantly swept aside this consensus. without legislative authority or public input, it redefined abortion as a va entitlement, including for dependents under the champva program. the proposed rollback returns policy to where congress left it: elective abortion is not health care, and the va is not in the business of elective terminations. moreover, polling has consistently shown that a strong majority of americans oppose taxpayer funding for abortion. the biden administration’s va policy ignored this reality and attempted to push a deeply controversial agenda through bureaucratic fiat. the proposed rule reflects the values of the veteran community and the american public. protecting veterans while preserving the va's mission opponents of the proposed rule have claimed, falsely, that it endangers the lives of pregnant veterans. this is fear-mongering, not fact. as the va has clarified, care for ectopic pregnancies, miscarriages, and life-threatening conditions was always covered under the medical benefits package—before and after the 2022 ifr. the proposed rule explicitly retains the life-of-the-mother exception. it ensures that women facing medical emergencies will receive the care they need. what it eliminates is the elective, on-demand abortion regime imposed in 2022, which was never medically justified and was legally suspect. veterans deserve a va system focused on their genuine health needs. the 2022 abortion expansion diverted limited resources from core missions, risked legal conflicts with state law, 8 and needlessly politicized veteran health care. this rule change restores balance, discipline, and focus to the va. champva and the abuse of federal programs the biden administration’s policy did not stop at veterans themselves—it extended abortion coverage to spouses, dependents, and caregivers under the champva program. this was a radical and unauthorized expansion of federal abortion funding, made even more egregious by the fact that champva is governed by statutory and regulatory constraints that mirror tricare. tricare does not cover elective abortions. neither should champva. the 2022 policy contradicted decades of precedent and inserted abortion into a family support program designed to help veterans' loved ones access health care. this distortion of champva’s purpose was both morally and legally indefensible. the proposed rule rightly reverses this abuse. reaffirming the proper role of federal agencies the 2022 va policy was part of a larger pattern during the biden administration: using the administrative state to advance a political ideology that lacked public and congressional support. from the eeoc to hhs to doe, the administration consistently pushed abortion mandates and stripped away religious liberty protections across federal programs. the va’s reversal represents a necessary rebalancing of power. agencies are not legislatures. they cannot invent entitlements, redefine statutory terms, or nullify conscience rights to serve ideological goals. this proposed rule sends a clear message that such abuses will not stand. conclusion the department of veterans affairs' proposed rule represents a pivotal opportunity to restore both the integrity of the agency and the constitutional rights of those who serve within it. by reversing the overreach of the 2022 interim final rule, the va will reestablish its rightful, limited role as a provider of essential health care—not an ideological enforcer of controversial social policy. the rule not only aligns the va’s policies with long-standing statutory restrictions and agency precedent, but also reflects the clear will of congress and the american people, who have consistently rejected the use of taxpayer dollars for elective abortion. importantly, this rule reinstates critical protections for conscience and religious freedom. the 2022 policy forced countless va personnel—doctors, nurses, chaplains, and administrators— into morally impossible situations by labeling abortion a “needed” service and failing to provide meaningful accommodations for those with religious or ethical objections. the cpac foundation’s center for regulatory freedom has consistently warned federal agencies that the suppression of religious dissent in service of political ideology not only violates constitutional protections, but threatens the moral credibility of our public institutions. the biden administration’s regulatory record reveals a broader pattern of contempt for conscience rights and statutory limits—from hhs’s conscience rule rescission, to eeoc’s distortion of the pregnant workers fairness act, to the department of education’s effort to strip protections from faith-based student groups. the va’s proposal to reject this approach is both timely and necessary. it affirms that the federal government has no legitimate authority to 9 redefine the meaning of medical necessity or override constitutional liberties by administrative fiat. for all these reasons, the center for regulatory freedom urges the department of veterans affairs to adopt this proposed rule in full and without delay. veterans and their families deserve a system of care rooted in medical necessity, legal clarity, and moral integrity—not one shaped by ideological expediency. finalizing this rule will help restore public trust in the va, reaffirm congressional authority, and uphold the foundational liberties that define american self- government. sincerely, andrew m. langer director cpac foundation center for regulatory freedom

department of veterans affairs 810 vermont avenue nw washington, d.c. 20420 re: comment regarding proposed rule: reproductive health services, docket no. va-2025-vha-0073, 90 fed. reg. 36415 (august 4, 2025) dear acting under secretary lieberman: vet voice foundation is a non-profit, non-partisan organization that seeks to empower veterans across the country to become civic leaders and policy advocates, harnessing the energy and drive of dedicated individuals who have fought for our country and putting it to work at home and in their communities on the important issues they face, including health care. this includes advocating for adequate and gender-specific health care for women veterans, who are the fastest growing population of veterans using veterans health administration (va) services. women are the fastest growing group in the veteran population, with an estimated population of over 2,000,000 women veterans in 2025. of the approximately 600,000 women veterans who access their health care through the va, half are of childbearing age. the women who access their health care services through the va are racially and ethnically diverse, with over 43 percent belonging to a racial or ethnic minority group. the share of family members accessing their health care through the civilian health and medical program of the department of veterans affairs (champva) has likewise increased in recent years. between fy2001 and fy2023, champva enrollments grew by 629%, from 96,500 to 703,600 beneficiaries. given these realities, it is crucial that the va maintain the medically necessary abortion care and counseling it currently provides. vet voice appreciates the opportunity to comment on va’s proposed rule on reproductive health services, docket no. va-2025-vha-0073 (the proposed rule), and writes in opposition to the proposed rule, which would modify the va’s medical benefits package by removing access to abortion care for veterans when the veteran’s health would be endangered if the pregnancy was carried to term and for veterans who became pregnant by rape or incest. the proposed rule likewise proposes eliminating access to any abortion counseling by va providers. the preamble to the proposed rule states that the va will continue to permit abortion care where a physician certifies that the life of the veteran would be endangered by the pregnancy, but does not propose codifying that exception or permit abortion counseling in those situations. the proposed rule rolls back access to abortion and abortion counseling for civilian health and medical program of the va (champva) beneficiaries by excluding abortion care where the health of the pregnant beneficiary would be endangered if the pregnancy were carried to term, or when the pregnancy is the result of an act of rape or incest. vet voice vehemently opposes the exclusions of abortion care and counseling in the proposed rule, which will harm the health and well-being of the veteran community and their beneficiaries. the proposed rule, and the legal interpretations espoused in it, are contrary to law and the relevant sources of statutory and regulatory authority that underlie the medical benefit programs for veterans and their beneficiaries. the va should withdraw its proposed rule. the va has the statutory authority to provide abortion care and counseling to veterans under 38 u.s.c. § 1710 and should continue to provide this essential and medically necessary care. pursuant to the va’s general-treatment authority for veterans, the va ‘‘shall furnish’’ certain veterans with ‘‘hospital care and medical services which the secretary determines to be needed.’’ the secretary ‘‘may,’’ subject to certain limitations, ‘‘furnish hospital care’’ and ‘‘medical services . . . which the secretary determines to be needed.’’ as relevant here, such ‘‘medical services’’ include ‘‘medical examination, treatment,’’ ‘‘[s]urgical services,’’ and ‘‘[p]reventive health services.’’ the va implements its general-treatment authority under 38 u.s.c. § 1710, and determines what care is ‘‘needed,’’ by regulation through the va’s medical benefits package. care included in the medical benefits package is ‘‘provided to individuals only if it is determined by appropriate health care professionals that the care is needed to promote, preserve, or restore the health of the individual and is in accord with generally accepted standards of medical practice.’’ in 2022, the va correctly determined that the following medical care and counseling is “needed” and authorized by the va’s general-treatment authority under 38 u.s.c. §1710(a): it is essential for the lives and health of our veterans that abortions be made available if determined needed by a health care professional when: (1) the life or health of the pregnant veteran would be endangered if the pregnancy were carried to term; or (2) the pregnancy is the result of an act of rape or incest. va has also determined that abortion counseling is needed so that veterans can make informed decisions about their health care. the va discussed the statutory support for its provision of such abortion care and counseling at length in its prior interim final rule (the 2022 ifr) and its 2024 final rule. the office of legal counsel likewise issued a still-binding opinion that under the va’s general-treatment authority, the va is authorized to provide abortion care and counseling specified in the 2022 ifr. the va’s proposed rule excludes abortions that a va clinician has determined to be medically necessary to preserve a woman’s health, and abortions for pregnancies that were the result of rape or incest. it also proposes excluding abortion counseling. the va justifies excluding this care in the proposed rule by stating that the 2022 ifr and final rule authorizing va to provide such abortion care and counseling were “legally questionable,” and claiming that va’s authority to provide abortions is “at least[] dubious and, at most, nonexistent.” these legal conclusions are inadequately explained and erroneous as a matter of statutory interpretation. to begin, in the proposed rule, the va does not expressly make a determination that abortion care and counseling services provided by the 2022 ifr are no longer “needed,” care and instead frames the changes in the proposed rule as a “decision to restore va’s medical benefits package to its pre-2022 state.” that is insufficient under the statute. the va previously determined that such abortion care and counseling were “needed,” under 38 u.s.c. § 1710, and unless and until the va makes an explicit determination that such care is “no longer needed,” supported by adequate evidence and consideration of the significant reliance interests at stake, the va “shall furnish” this care under its general-treatment authority. if the proposed rule becomes final based on this ill-explained and erroneous legal interpretation, it will be contrary to law. the va claims, without support, that “[c]onsiderations about whether abortion is ‘needed’ for purposes of va- provided services necessarily involves the question of whether taxpayers should pay for abortion.” that novel assertion finds no support in the statutory text of section 1710 or in any of va’s previous interpretations of its general-treatment authority. to the contrary, as the va previously explained, in passing the vhca, congress intended that the va’s determination of whether certain care should be provided would be based only on whether that care is medically necessary. whether and to what extent taxpayers are funding care for veterans is irrelevant to whether such care is medically necessary. the va makes no attempt to explain this novel interpretation, and the statutory text certainly does not provide a basis for the va’s erroneous interpretation of when and why care is medically necessary under its regulations. finally, the proposed rule vaguely refers to the hyde amendment and other similar statutory provisions that restrict when federal funds can be used for abortion as a potential justification for drawing “a bright line between elective abortion and health care services that taxpayers would support.” but this does not provide the support the proposed rule claims. to the contrary, the existence of other restrictions on abortions demonstrates that congress has made a consistent choice for 50 years not to apply the hyde amendment or any other statutory restriction to the va. it also underscores that the proposed rule’s exclusion of abortions for pregnancies that are the result of rape and incest is not only cruel but inconsistent with the congressional judgment that such abortions should be paid for with federal funds. at bottom, the proposed rule’s failure to assess that excluded abortion care and counseling are no longer “needed,” and its reliance on inapplicable legal restrictions lay bare that the proposed rule is a not-so-thinly-veiled attempt to limit medically necessary abortions because of a policy disagreement with this care. but congress determined that medical necessity, not policy objections, is the standard by which va determines whether it will provide medical care to those who have served our nation. section 106 of the vhca does not prohibit the abortion care and counseling provided by the 2022 ifr and final rule. the proposed rule tepidly states that section 106 of the vhca may call into question the va’s general-treatment authority under section 1710 to provide abortion care and counseling. not only is this conclusion inadequately stated and explained, but any conclusion that section 106 somehow prohibits the provision of abortion care and counseling in the 2022 ifr is legally erroneous as a matter of statutory interpretation. any final rule cannot rely on the va’s flawed interpretation of section 106 espoused in the proposed rule. first, the va does not make clear in the proposed rule what authority it relies on in excluding the abortion care and counseling provided in the 2022 ifr from va’s medical benefits package. as explained above, the va previously relied on its general-treatment authority under section 1710 as the basis for its determination in the 2022 ifr and final rule that such abortion care and counseling was needed and therefore must be included in its medical benefits package. if va believes that it did not previously have the legal authority to provide certain abortion care and counseling under section 1710, it must say so and adequately explain its changed legal interpretation of that provision. the proposed rule certainly does not do so. the proposed rule appears to rely on section 106’s exclusion of abortion-related services as authorizing its exclusion of abortion care and counseling, asserting that “our actions fully comply with its abortion exclusion.” what “exclusion” the va is referring to is unclear. on that basis, the proposed rule claims that “va’s authority to provide abortions is, at least, dubious and, at most, nonexistent.” to the extent that the va is relying on section 106 as providing statutory authority for its exclusion of abortion care and counseling from its medical benefits package, that conclusion is contrary to law and va’s long-standing interpretation of section 106 dating back to 1993. to state it clearly, va has already made clear that it does not rely on section 106 to provide any care—pregnancy or otherwise. as explained in more detail below, the va cannot rely on a non-operative provision (section 106) as supporting its prohibition in the proposed rule on the provision of certain abortion care and counseling under its general-treatment authority in section 1710. as the va previously and correctly concluded, section 106 of the vhca does not prohibit va’s from providing abortion care and counseling in its medical benefits package. prior to the 1996 enactment of the vhca, va health care was subject to a patchwork of eligibility criteria, and care was largely linked only to medical care of service-connected conditions. the vhca, in relevant part, was designed to improve the health care services available to women veterans. section 106(a) of the vhca stated that va could provide ‘‘women’’ with ‘‘[p]apanicolaou tests (pap smears),’’ ‘‘[b]reast examinations and mammography,’’ and ‘‘[g]eneral reproductive health care . . . , but not including under this section infertility services, abortions, or pregnancy care (including prenatal and delivery care), except for such care relating to a pregnancy that is complicated or in which the risks of complication are increased by a service-connected condition.’’ relevant here, the vhca made the availability of all medical care services for veterans turn on a single “need for care” criterion focusing on medical judgment rather than legal definitions. that is because prior to the 1996 act, section 1710 only addressed eligibility for hospital, nursing, and domiciliary care. it did not address outpatient medical services, which were instead covered by section 1712. that section authorized the secretary to provide “such [ambulatory or outpatient] medical services as the secretary determines are needed,” but “require[d] the va to apply at least four different legal tests to distinct veteran classifications” using “medically uninterpretable” standards. for instance, one provision required care where it would “obviate the need for hospital admission.” in the 1996 act, congress repealed section 1712, and the confusing “legal tests” contained within that provision, and instead provided a single “need for care” determination. the congressional record accompanying the 1996 act is clear that the purpose of the act was to create a more streamlined and medically grounded criterion for determining what care should be provided to veterans. the house report accompanying the act summarizes congress’ view of what the 1996 act meant to achieve: “while the new standard is a simple one, more importantly, it would employ a clinically appropriate ‘need for care’ test, thereby ensuring that medical judgment rather than legal criteria will determine when care will be provided and the level at which that care will be furnished.” the amendments would “establish medical need as the sole criterion of eligibility for va hospital care and medical services.” thus, the vhca “overtook section 106 of the vhca.” as the va explained at length in the 2022 ifr and final rule, the exclusion of certain abortion care in section 106 does “not limit va’s authority to provide care under any other provision of law,” including its general-treatment authority under 38 u.s.c. § 1710. the va stated that “it has consistently interpreted section 106 in this fashion,” and unequivocally stated that “va no longer relies on section 106 of the vhca to provide such services or any other services.” rather, as the va explained, it “relies on 38 u.s.c. 1710(a)(1)–(3) to provide pap smears, breast exams and mammography, or general reproductive health services, [and] pregnancy or infertility services.” thus, section 106’s “prohibition on providing certain services,” including abortions, “simply is no longer operative.” notably, the va has long exercised its general-treatment authority to provide comprehensive pregnancy care and infertility without opposition or argument that it acted contrary to section 106. a veteran in 1992 was only eligible for pregnancy and delivery care under section 106 if the pregnancy was complicated or the risks of complication were increased by a service-connected condition. pub. l. no. 102-585, § 106(a). in contrast, general pregnancy and delivery services were included in the medical benefits package when it was established in 1999 pursuant to va’s authority in 38 u.s.c. § 1710. moreover, while section 106 of the vhca provided that infertility services could not be provided under that section, infertility services (with the exception of in vitro fertilization) were also included in the medical benefits package pursuant to va’s authority under 38 u.s.c. § 1710. and in 2017, the secretary authorized the provision of in vitro fertilization (ivf) treatment for veterans in certain cases, notwithstanding the exclusion of such care under section 106 of the 1992 act. consequently, for decades, va has offered general pregnancy care and certain infertility services under 38 u.s.c. § 1710. there is no argument—and the va has never taken the position—that general pregnancy care or ivf services are foreclosed by section 106. rather the “under this section” language in section 106 preserved the authority of the secretary to provide such care if and when he deemed it “needed,” including as va has historically done, under its general treatment authority. the proposed rule does not meaningfully grapple with the va’s long standing, extensive, careful, and contrary interpretation of section 106 in the 2022 ifr and final rule. nor does it grapple with the olc’s still-binding conclusion that section 106 does not prohibit va from providing such care under its general-treatment authority. the proposed rule acknowledges that “the wholesale revision” in the vhca “may limit the continued force and effect of section 106,” but nonetheless states that the exclusions in the proposed rule “fully comply with its abortion exclusion.” to the extent that the proposed rule is relying on section 106 as providing authority for its exclusion of abortion care and counseling from its medical benefits package, it must say so clearly in the final rule. but to the extent that the final rule relies on section 106 as authorizing the exclusions on abortion care and counseling, such an interpretation is both contrary to law and an unexplained change from the va’s long-standing interpretation that section 106 is no longer operative and is not the basis on which it provides women with pregnancy care. it is also an interpretation that would conflict the va’s longstanding practice of providing general pregnancy and fertility services in its medical benefits package pursuant to its general-treatment authority. section 106 does not prohibit the abortion care and counseling provided in the 2022 ifr and final rule and cannot serve as the basis for any prohibitions of such care in a final rule. the secretary has the authority to provide coverage for abortion care and counseling for champva beneficiaries. by statute, va’s ‘‘secretary is authorized to provide’’ specified ‘‘medical care’’ to certain spouses, children, survivors, and caregivers of veterans who meet specific eligibility criteria. this health benefits program is known as champva. va must provide ‘‘for medical care’’ under champva ‘‘in the same or similar manner and subject to the same or similar limitations as medical care is’’ provided by the department of defense to active-duty family members, retired service members and their families, and others under the tricare (select) program. va has regulated services covered by champva to mean those medical services that are medically necessary and appropriate for the treatment of a condition and that are not specifically excluded. prior to 2022, champva coverage significantly deviated from its statutory mandate that it provide the same or similar care as the tricare program because champva did not provide for abortion counseling and did not provide for abortions when the pregnancy is the result of rape or incest. in 2022, the va amended its champva regulations by “removing the exclusion for abortion counseling and permitting abortions when the health of the pregnant beneficiary would be endangered if the pregnancy were carried to term, or when the pregnancy is the result of an act of rape or incest.” va did so, in part, to “better align coverage under champva with coverage under tricare (select).” then and now, tricare provides coverage for abortions when the pregnancy is the result of for rape and incest or where a physician certifies that the life of the woman would be endangered if the fetus were carried to term. tricare also provides counseling for covered abortions. thus, the va’s 2022 amendment of the champva regulations brought that program in alignment with its statutory mandate to provide benefits that are the same or similar to those offered by the tricare program. in the proposed rule, the va concludes that “abortion is not a ‘needed’ va service for the same reasons that it is not ‘medically necessary and appropriate for the treatment of a condition’ under champva.” again, the proposed rule has made no finding, supported by evidence, that champva coverage provided by the 2022 ifr and final rule is not medically necessary. the proposed rule does not explain the va’s change in position that such abortion care and counseling is not medically necessary under section 1781, much less rebut va’s previous conclusions supported by data that such abortion care and counseling provided by the 2022 ifr and final rule was medically necessary. the proposed rule thus does not align with the statutory mandate that the va provide abortion care under champva that is medically necessary by permitting abortions when the health of the pregnant beneficiary would be endangered if the pregnancy were carried to term, or when the pregnancy is the result of an act of rape or incest. additionally, although the va correctly acknowledges that champva coverage need not be identical to that offered under tricare, the proposed rule does not otherwise address or acknowledge the significant differences that would be created between tricare and champva coverage if a final rule excludes abortion counseling and abortions that are necessary for pregnancies that result from rape or incest. if adopted into a final rule, such a difference in coverage would run afoul of the statutory mandate that champva provide medically necessary coverage that is the same or similar as that provided by tricare. for these reasons, vet voice foundation strongly opposes the proposed rule and the va should withdraw the proposed rule. very respectfully, janessa goldbeck chief executive officer vet voice foundation

health and supports access to the full continuum of reproductive health care, including stabilizing emergency treatments such as abortion. hadassah strongly opposes the u.s. department of veterans affairs’ (va) proposed rule (rin 2900-as31) on reproductive health services, which will lead to worse physical and mental health outcomes for veterans, including survivors of sexual assault, jeopardize the life, health and future fertility of pregnant people, and place unfair financial burdens on women servicemembers and veterans. the va’s proposed rule,1 reinstates the full exclusion on abortions and abortion counseling, eliminating exceptions for rape, incest and the health of the mother. according to the va’s own guidance, the veteran’s medical benefits package should include care and services that “prevent future health problems” and “enhance […] quality of life.”2 however, if the proposed rule is promulgated and implemented, it will jeopardize the health, well-being and fertility capacity of veterans, in direct conflict with these health benefits. this is especially devastating given the sacrifices our veterans and their families have made to serve and protect our country. it is our responsibility to protect the freedoms, rather than interfere with their right to access quality and safe reproductive health care. as the largest integrated health system in the country, restrictions on access to reproductive health care in the veterans health system will be devastating for the two million female veterans3 who have served our country, particularly the 43% of women veterans using va health care who are of reproductive age.4 1 reproductive health services; department of veterans affairs 2025, 90 fed. reg. 36415 2 u.s. department of veterans affairs. about va health benefits. https://www.va.gov/health-care/about- va-health-benefits/. 3 u.s. department of veterans affairs. women veterans health care.
